Sign in with your email and password, or with Google when your deployment offers it, then choose the instance you work in. FACE opens on Ask.
The app opens on the sign-in page. Any page you open while signed out also brings you here, and so does a session that ends or that the server rejects.
data.choose-an-instance#Choose an instance:
After a successful sign-in you land on SELECT INSTANCE.
With Google, select the Google button and complete Google’s own dialog. A browser that is already signed in to Google may complete the sign-in without asking.
data.choose-an-instance-1#Choose an instance:
An instance is the FACE deployment you are working in. The SELECT INSTANCE page (Choose an active instance to continue.) lists every instance your account has a grant on, under Choose an instance. The refresh button (Refresh instances) reads the list again.
Each card shows:
the product and the instance name; the tenant; your role: Admin, Editor, Viewer or Service account; the status; how long your access lasts, for example Access does not expire. A card marked Current is the instance you are already using. Anything the server did not report is shown as not stated, for example Role not stated.
Select a card to open it, even when it is the only one. FACE then reads the instance’s posture and opens Ask. Your role on the instance decides whether you see the Admin entry under Settings › Account. To switch instance later, select the instance chip in the rail footer.
data.complete-the-second-factor-if-asked#Comp: If your account has an authenticator enrolled, the app opens the MFA page (see below).
data.enter-your-email-and-password#Enter your: Type your address in Email and your password in Password. The eye button (Show password / Hide password) reveals what you typed. Press Enter in the email field to move to the password field.
data.rpcs-behind-these-pages#RPCs behind thes: IdentityService.Login: password, Google and the second-factor step. IdentityService.Logout. runink.ui.profile.v1.ProfileService.ListInstances: the instance list. See the API reference.
data.select-sign-in#Select Sign In: Or press Enter in the password field. While the server checks your credentials, the button shows a spinner. Screen readers announce it as Signing in.
data.sign-in-methods#Sign-in methods:
When the page loads, the app asks the backend which sign-in methods it offers. The backend answers on its /auth/config endpoint.
Method When it appears Email and Password Always. Google single sign-on Only when the backend reports Google sign-in as configured. An or divider separates it from the password form. If the app cannot reach the sign-in service, the Google button is replaced by Single sign-on is unavailable — the sign-in service could not be reached. You can still sign in with your email and password. If the backend reports that it has no single sign-on, the page shows no Google button and no message.
data.signing-out#Signing out: Sign out with Log out at the foot of the rail, or under Settings › Account. Signing out closes any dialogs that were open and returns you to this page.
data.two-factor-verification#Two-factor verif:
The MFA Verification page asks you to Enter the 6-digit code from your authenticator. Type the code into the six boxes. The code is submitted as soon as the last digit is in. Screen readers announce Verifying code while it is checked.
Cancel / Return to Login abandons the attempt. You can only reach this page while a second-factor challenge is waiting. Otherwise the app sends you back to sign-in.
data.when-the-list-is-empty-or-fails#When the: You see Meaning What to do No instance grants you access — Ask an admin of the instance you need to invite you. The server answered and you hold no grant on any instance. Ask an admin of that instance to invite you. This deployment has no instances to choose from. The deployment itself offers no instances. Ask your platform operator. Could not be read, followed by a reason and Retry The list could not be read. This does not mean you have no instances. Read the reason, then select Retry.

data: FACE tells two situations apart. It could not look: the request failed, so nothing is known. Or it looked and found nothing: the answer came back and was empty. The messages below are the exact English wording. Check which of the two a message describes before you act on it.
data.ask#Ask: Message What it means What to do Switched off: not read by Fetch An admin switched this connection off, so no run reads it. Ask an admin to switch it back on, under How FACE knows this on Ask. {name} was not switched: {error} The Active switch could not be saved. Read the reason. Only an admin can switch a connection or runner. Offline mode: Fetch task queued for background synchronization. The app could not reach the server, so it kept the run on your device. Nothing. The run is sent when the connection returns. Offline queueing failed: {error} The run could not even be queued. Try again once you are back online. No result received The run ended without a final answer. Open the run to read what arrived, then ask again. Your last fetch failed. The last run did not complete. Select Open the run and read Result and Error. Your last fetch answered, but not every phase finished. The answer came back, and a phase after it did not finish. The message names which, and why. Pages that phase feeds say so for this run. Ask again, or open an earlier Successful run. Failed to load fetch starters The prepared questions could not be loaded. Type your question instead. This run is no longer in your history. The run was deleted from this device. Run it again.
data.automated-analysis#Automated analysis: Message What it means What to do Automated analysis is starting up… The analysis models are loading. Everything else works now. Wait, then select Check again. Automated analysis is not ready — features that need it are unavailable. The analysis service cannot answer. Select Check again. If it persists, see Operating FACE.
data.no-data-yet#No data yet: Message What it means What to do Nothing is connected yet No data source is attached to this instance, so there is nothing to assess. Add one under Settings › Integrations › Systems. No data source is configured yet. The source list was read and is empty. Select Connect a data source. Could not load your data sources. The source list could not be read. Select Retry. Your operation’s story starts with a fetch No run is selected, so the page has nothing to show. Ask a question on Ask, or select Open an earlier run. Run a fetch first — the compliance twin analyzes that instance’s real findings, not a blank prompt. The remediation screens analyse a run’s findings, and none has finished yet. Run a question on Ask first. Unable to Assess The twin answered, but could not produce an assessment. This is not a clean result. Read the summary for the reason. Usually you need to connect a data source and run again.
data.options-why-and-actionable-twins#Options: Message What it means What to do Failed to fetch action queue: {error} The decisions on Actionable Twins could not be read. The list may not be empty. Select Refresh. The map could not be loaded: {reason} The Map view could not read where your assets are. Read the reason, then open the Map view again. Live layers could not be read: {reason} The map’s live connection layers could not be read. Your own assets may still show. Check the connections are active, then open the Map view again. That file is too large to analyze (3 MB maximum). The file for Analyze document is over the limit. Split or reduce the file. Could not read that file. The browser could not read the chosen file. Pick the file again. Could not load scenarios The scenarios could not be read. Select Retry. Failed to extract rules: {error} The rules could not be read. Select Retry on Why. The options could not be compared: {error} Options could not compare the options for a decision. Nothing is shown in their place. Try again.
data.signing-in#Signing in: Message What it means What to do Single sign-on is unavailable — the sign-in service could not be reached. You can still sign in with your email and password. The app could not reach the sign-in service’s configuration. Sign in with your email and password, or try again later. The server did not accept these credentials. The email or password was rejected. Check both and try again. Invalid two-factor code The code from your authenticator was wrong or out of date. Wait for the next code and enter it. MFA session expired — please sign in again The second-factor challenge timed out. Sign in again from the start. This account is not authorized for this instance Your account is valid but has no access to this instance. Ask an admin of the instance to invite you. Session expired — please sign in again Your session ended. Sign in again. No instance grants you access You signed in, but you hold no grant on any instance. Ask an admin to invite you. Could not be read, on the instance picker The instance list could not be read. This does not mean you have none. Select Retry.
data.still-stuck#Still stuck: For problems on the deployment side, see Operating FACE.
data.voice#Voice: Message What it means What to do Voice input is unavailable in this browser or the microphone was blocked. Type your question instead. The browser has no speech support, or microphone access was refused. Allow the microphone for FACE’s site in your browser settings, or type instead.

data:
Why tells you what is happening and what is causing it, for the selected run. It answers the run’s question first, then shows every check FACE ran on the rows the run read, what your records and public pages say about each counterparty, and the business rules behind it all. Open it with Why, under Simulate in the rail (/simulate?tab=knowledge).
Every figure on Why is measured on the rows the selected run read. A figure that could not be measured says so and why. It is never shown as zero.
data.counterparty-reviews#Counterparty review:
Counterparty reviews covers the carriers, shippers, buyers, sellers, distribution centres and logistics providers your data names. For each it shows what your own records say (shipments, claims, invoices over contract) and what public web pages say, with each red flag citing its page.
No cited red flag in the pages found. That clears no one. The searches returned no pages. That clears no one. Public reviews not searched: the run’s rows state no name for this party, and FACE does not search the web by an internal id. This is not a background check.
data.decide-the-enforcement#Decide the enforc: Choose an Enforcement action: Audit only, Review required or Block. Optionally fill in Tolerance (in the rule’s own units), Policy reference (the clause you cite) and Rationale (why, for the reviewer).
data.how-face-knows-this#How FACE knows this:
How FACE knows this (The rows behind each figure, the rules FACE read and their policies) is folded at the foot of the page. It holds:
The rows behind the figures: the board’s views over the rows it read, per carrier, claim, invoice and stock position; the rules FACE read from your systems, counted apart from the checks: RULES HOLDING IN THE DATA and RULES BROKEN; Rules your operations run on, described below.
data.open-the-policy-editor#Open the policy e: Select the tune button on a rule (Open the policy editor). The Enforcement policy drawer opens below it.
data.rpcs-behind-this-page#RPCs behind this p: FetchService.GetOperationsBoard, for the money, the board and the checks. RulesService.AnalyzeCode, UpdateRulePolicy. PostureService.GetHealthScore. See the API reference.
data.rules-and-policies#Rules your operations:
Rules your operations run on (Your business rules, checked against what your systems actually do and against the policy documents you add) lists the business rules FACE found and the ones you added. All domains ({count}) and the domain pills narrow the list. These are your business’s rules, not FACE’s own guard rules, which are on Admin.
Every rule carries one verdict, each with its own glyph and word, so it never depends on colour alone:
Verdict Meaning Aligned Aligned with policy. Drift Drifted: needs reconciliation. Shadow Undocumented. Missing Missing: needs reconciliation. Unrated No verdict was returned yet.
data.save-policy#Save policy:
Save policy stays disabled until you choose an action. The drawer records who set it and when. The policy was not saved keeps your entries so you can try again. Discard drops your changes.
Saving a rule’s enforcement validates it. A validated rule goes to the simulations on Options by itself, and the twins are re-run for your instance. Include this rule in Simulate takes a rule in or out of that selection.
The drawer also holds the Reconcile inspector: a read-only comparison of Actual — implementation against Intended — policy. Nothing to compare yet means FACE captured neither for the rule.
In an open rule’s drawer, Edit & Reconcile opens the rule (Rule Name, Logic (Plain English), then Save Rule), and Ignore sets it aside. Unsaved marks a rule you edited or added here until you save a policy on it. Under the list, Create New Business Rule… adds a rule in plain English.
data.the-answer#The answer:
The page opens with one sentence that answers the run’s question, from the check that answers it. A stockout question, for example, is answered by the stock checks. The answer states the money the failing rows put at stake ({amount} at stake), the cause in plain words, and the worst rows first (Worst first). Two ways on follow: See options opens Options on that decision, and Act in Actionable Twins opens the decisions.
When no check answers the question directly, the answer says No check this run measured answers the question directly. The largest thing needing attention: and names the thing with the most money on it: a failing check, the deductions open more than 60 days, or the claims whose window closes within 14 days. Nothing on this run needs attention. means the run measured nothing that needs saying.
data.the-money-and-the-checks#The money and t:
Under the answer are the same money tiles as on Ask, in the same words: At risk, Owed to you, Claim windows closing in 14 days and Shipments at risk, each with its change since the last run. A line counts the checks, {total} checks: {failing} failing, {holding} holding, {notMeasured} not measured.
The operations board follows, with four figures measured on the run’s rows:
Figure Detail On-time delivery How many of the delivered shipments were on time, and how many are overdue Open claims How many close within 14 days, and how many were filed after the window Invoices over contract How many of the invoices checked bill above the contract, and by how much Stock below reorder point How many positions are below their reorder point, and how many below safety stock Each figure states its basis, for example over every row read, or Sample figure, not a total when the run read a sample. Overdue and days left are measured as of the data’s latest row read, not the time of the run.
data.what-face-checked#What FACE checked:
What FACE checked lists every check run on the rows the selected run read, each once: failing checks first, the most money then the most rows. Holding ({count}) and Not measured ({count}) are folded below them.
A failing check says what does not hold, for example Deliveries late against their promise, and how many rows: {failing} of {checked} rows checked do not hold, with the money its rows put at risk when they state any. Open it to see its rows. A check that held only in a sample says a sample, not a pass.
The checks cover deliveries and promises, claims and their windows, deductions, invoices against the contract, rate contracts, stock, bills of lading and proofs of delivery, customs, insurance and cover, and deadlines and signatures. Each check carries the Twins category it belongs to.
For: narrows the list to an audience: Everyone, Paralegals (bills of lading, deadlines, signatures and the claim file’s documents) or Brokers & underwriters (customs and cover). A deadline here is an input to a person, not legal advice.
Above the list, anything that blocks a decision is said first: rules that disagree with what your systems do, rules that could not be read, and values read from the run’s documents that fail a check (Correct them where the run shows what it was given.).
data.what-this-run-was-given#What this run wa: What this run was given opens the run’s own page, where the files and captures attached to it are listed with how each was read. See Open a past run.

data:
FACE starts from the systems you already run: warehouses and databases, ERPs and SaaS platforms, files and buckets, event buses, telemetry from pallets, readers and trucks, and camera feeds. You add each one as a connection in Settings › Integrations › Systems, then choose it as a source on Ask or in a brief. Every connection must be encrypted, with a login where the protocol has one: FACE refuses one that is not.
This section describes each connector: the settings a connection takes, how credentials are held, what Test checks, and what Explore and Sample return. Live connection types (cameras, sensors, field readers) open their live view from the connection’s card on Ask. See Connections and credentials.
data.connector-families#Connector families: Connections and credentialsWhere to add and choose them, security rules, credentials, Test semantics QuickstartsThe quickstart estate: a dataset to load and fetch for all 32 connection types, and every connector at once Explore, sample and profileWhat metadata is read, and which values may leave a source SQL warehouses and databasesSnowflake, Databricks, PostgreSQL, MySQL Enterprise SaaS and ERPSAP, Salesforce, Guidewire, ServiceNow, Google Workspace Files and object storageExcel, CSV/JSON/Parquet objects, S3, GCS, Azure Blob, document sources Streaming: KafkaTopic catalogue and Schema Registry Event listenersChanges from PostgreSQL and Kafka that trigger analysis TelemetryMQTT 3.1.1 over TLS, RFID (LLRP and REST), GPS, Modbus-TCP Logistics systems of recordOMS, TMS, WMS, YMS, IMS, WHS and more over REST CCTV and videoRTSPS, ONVIF over HTTPS, snapshots, device capture Flipper edge readerHandheld field readings through the edge agent Web and crawlerOne page as text, and bounded crawls RunnersWhere queries run, and keeping data in your network Networking and address policyIPv6-first, Happy Eyeballs, refused addresses TroubleshootingThe errors connectors return, and what to do
data.how-to-read-this-section#How to read thi:
Every connector page answers the same four questions:
Which type spellings resolve. FACE lowercases the connection type and strips spaces, underscores and hyphens before looking it up, so Service Now, service-now and servicenow are the same type. Which settings and credentials it reads. Settings are ordinary fields on the connection record. Secrets are kept in a sealed credential bundle and are never returned. See Connections and credentials. What Test does. Some connectors dial the source. Others can only save the configuration. The response tells you which through live_check_performed, and each page says what a successful probe does not establish. What Explore and Sample return. Explore reads catalogue metadata only. Sample reads a bounded set of real rows, one dataset at a time. See Explore, sample and profile.
data.implementation-principles#Implementation: Every connection is encrypted. TLS with the certificate checked, and a login where the protocol has one. A connection that does not meet this cannot be saved, and a stored one is refused until it is upgraded. See Security requirements. Wire protocols are implemented natively. MQTT, LLRP, Modbus-TCP, the Kafka handshake, RTSP and ONVIF are written directly against the wire format. FACE adds no third-party protocol library for them. An empty answer is never a silent success. When a telemetry or system-of-record connector connects and receives nothing, it reports Success=false and names what it listened to. It does not return an empty table. Absence stays absent. When a source does not state a threshold, a unit or a row count, FACE leaves the value unset. It does not fill in a plausible default. Every read is bounded. Every connector caps its collection windows, record counts, page counts and body sizes. When a read hits a cap, the result is marked as truncated. Observed lineage records structure only. Every extraction through the connector registry writes a lineage record with column names, counts, durations and a query shape. The record never includes result values or credentials.

data:
A camera is a data source in FACE. It can be an IP camera or NVR over RTSPS, an ONVIF device over HTTPS, an HTTPS feed, a video file, or the operator’s own device camera pushing frames. You add it in Settings › Integrations › Systems. Its card on Ask then opens Surveillance, the live feed, with that camera already chosen.
The connector’s job is reachability and description. Frame analysis happens in FACE’s vision pipeline (see /docs/analysis/).
data.explore-asking-the-camera-what-it-is#Exp:
Endpoint Explore reads rtsps:// Native RTSP OPTIONS + DESCRIBE (Accept: application/sdp). There is one dataset per media track, with codec, clock rate, packetisation and profile, plus resolution and frame rate where the camera states them, including from the H.264 parameter sets. https:// (ONVIF) ONVIF over SOAP 1.2: GetSystemDateAndTime, GetDeviceInformation, GetServices/GetCapabilities, GetProfiles, GetVideoSourceConfigurations and GetStreamUri. Each returned stream URI is then described over RTSP in the same call. You type a host and a credential, and FACE finds the streams. File path, device capture supported=false, with the reason CCTVService.DescribeSource returns the same description for an ad-hoc endpoint. Each reason repeats what a DESCRIBE does not establish:
that video is being published (an NVR describes a channel whose camera is unplugged) that the codec will decode on this deployment that the scene is what you expect that playback (SETUP/PLAY) will be allowed ONVIF uses Media ver10. A device that serves profiles only on Media2 reports zero profiles, and the reason says so. FACE does not multicast-probe your LAN (WS-Discovery) and does not subscribe to events. Each camera is added by address.
data.frame-limits#Frame limits: Accepted formats: JPEG and PNG (unsupported image format "…" (only jpeg/png accepted)) At most 12 MiB per frame, and 40 million pixels Frames sampled from a feed per sweep are set by the operator setting VISION_SWEEP_FRAMES. A camera connection’s Execute has no tabular result and says so. Frames reach analysis through the ingest path, not through SqlService.
data.frames-two-paths#Frames: two paths: Path RPC What it does What it leaves behind Graded SurveillanceService.IngestSurveillanceFeed (and a fetch’s camera branch) Samples or receives frames, then runs the vision tier: object grading, material, damage, and evidence frames One lineage record per ingest, evidence artefacts, observations Live SurveillanceService.DetectLiveFrame One validated frame through the deployment’s local detector only. It never reaches the vision model or the network. Shown on Surveillance; not stored as an observation or evidence A live answer carries box_origin = BOX_ORIGIN_LOCAL_DETECTOR, the detector’s own label, and no grade, material or damage fields. Its detection_note is never empty and says whether a local detector is present in this deployment. That note describes the deployment, not the camera.
data.settings-cctvconnectionconfig#Settings (:
Setting Meaning endpoint_url rtsps:// or https://, or a file path readable on the processing node. rtsp:// and http:// are refused, because they are unencrypted. Do not put credentials in the URL. username Camera username (a setting) max_frames Frames sampled per extraction. 0 means the server default, not “none”. transport RTSP transport: tcp (default) or udp device_capture Marks a push source: the operator’s device records frames and sends them to FACE. endpoint_url stays empty. Credential: password. It answers RTSP Digest (preferred) or Basic challenges, and ONVIF WS-Security UsernameToken with a password digest. It is never echoed, logged or written into lineage.
Cameras live on site networks. Set allow_internal_network to control whether a connection may reach internal addresses.
data.snapshots#Snapshots: When a camera supports ONVIF GetSnapshotUri, FACE can fetch a still with one authenticated GET instead of decoding video. Only the path and query from the device’s answer are used. The host and port stay the ones on your connection, so a device cannot redirect FACE to another address. The response must validate as an image.
data.test#Test:
Test on a camera connection, from Settings › Integrations › Systems, uses this probe:
Endpoint What Test does rtsps:// TCP connect to the camera (5 s) https:// One HEAD request with the credentials. 401/403 is reported as feed rejected the credentials (HTTP …). File path Checks that the file exists and is not a directory Device capture Validates the configuration. There is no server-side endpoint to dial. device_capture together with an endpoint_url is refused. A successful probe says the camera accepted a connection. It does not say that video is being published or that a frame will decode.
data.type-spellings#Type spellings: Where Spellings Connector registry (Test, Explore) cctv, videostream (video_stream, the “Video Stream” card), camera Fetch routing cctv, video_stream, videostream, camera, webcam

data: You add a connection once, in Settings › Integrations › Systems, and then choose it as a source wherever you ask a question: on Ask, and per brief on Briefs. FACE refuses any connection that would send data or a credential unencrypted.
data.connection-strings#Connection strings:
For snowflake and databricks you can paste a connection string in the connection_string property. FACE parses it at save time:
The settings it names become typed settings. The string wins for every setting it states. Settings it does not state keep what the form carried. The secret it contains goes to the credential bundle under the connector’s normal key. The raw string itself is not kept. If the string cannot be parsed, the save fails, so you find out when you paste, not at the next fetch. For Snowflake, a DSN field that FACE does not carry is refused rather than dropped silently. So is an explicit host that disagrees with the account. For other types, a connection_string credential is left in the bundle untouched. The Azure object store reads it from there.
data.creating-listing-and-deleting#Creating,:
Create. CreateConnection takes the Connection and a credentials map. FACE writes the credential bundle first and then the record. If writing the credentials fails, no connection is created, and the response carries success: false with the underlying message. The response echoes connection_id either way, so a retry does not create a second row.
List. ListConnections returns every connection with two annotations and a warnings list:
credential_state tells you what this node holds:
Value Meaning CREDENTIAL_STATE_PRESENT A bundle was found and opened on this node. Nothing was dialled, so an expired password still reads PRESENT. CREDENTIAL_STATE_NONE_NEEDED The catalogue says this type reads no secret, for example Excel. This is a normal state. CREDENTIAL_STATE_ABSENT There is no bundle for a type that expects one. FACE cannot tell “never entered” apart from “not present on this node”. CREDENTIAL_STATE_UNREADABLE A bundle exists and could not be opened. Re-entering the credential does not fix a key problem. CREDENTIAL_STATE_UNSPECIFIED Not computed. This value is not “present” or “absent”. The fetch pipeline uses the same classifier, so the list and a fetch always agree. Opening a present bundle is recorded in the credential audit trail.
source_backing is covered below.
warnings carries plain-language conditions about the list itself, such as storage durability. Show them as written. They are not failures.
Delete. DeleteConnection answers with an explicit outcome:
outcome Meaning DELETE_CONNECTION_OUTCOME_DELETED The credential bundle was removed first, then the record. DELETE_CONNECTION_OUTCOME_NOT_FOUND This instance holds no such id. Nothing was deleted. DELETE_CONNECTION_OUTCOME_FAILED The delete was attempted and failed. message carries the error, and the connection may still exist. An empty id also returns this, with no connection id provided. success is true only for DELETED. Deleting a connection does not revoke the credential at its issuer, and it does not rewrite fetch definitions or lineage that reference the id.
data.observed-lineage#Observed lineage:
Every connector returned by the registry is wrapped by a lineage recorder. Each extraction appends a record to an append-only log. The record contains:
column names counts and durations a literal-free query shape and its fingerprint a closed-set error class A record never contains result values, driver messages or credentials. Camera ingests are recorded separately (one record per ingest, with a row count of zero, because a camera sends frames rather than rows). Lineage is visible in source activity. See /docs/analysis/.
data.secrets-never-stay-on-the-record#Secrets:
Several configuration messages still have secret-looking fields (password, client_secret, personal_access_token, service_account_json, api_key, security_token). When a connection is created, FACE reads those fields, moves them into the credential bundle, and never writes them back out. A connection you read back through ListConnections has those fields empty. That is by design.
Credentials are stored encrypted and never returned by the API. The internal record type has no field that can hold a secret, and secrets placed in the free-form properties map are rejected.
Connectors read their secrets only from the credential bundle they are handed. Setting a password on the record has no effect.
data.security-requirements#Security requireme:
Every connection must use encrypted transport with the server’s certificate checked, and a login wherever the protocol has one. This is not a setting you can turn off. The server enforces it in four places:
Save. CreateConnection and updates refuse an insecure connection before anything is written, with InvalidArgument: this connection cannot be saved without its security settings: . Test. TestConnection on a draft that would be refused dials nothing and answers nothing was dialled: …. Every read of a stored connection. Fetch, Explore, discovery, data listeners, live sensors, document ingest and Test all refuse a stored connection that fails the policy, with FailedPrecondition: this connection is not secured: ; open it in Settings › Integrations and upgrade its security. The stored connection is kept as it is. Nothing rewrites or deletes it. List. ListConnections sets security_ok and security_problems on each connection. The connection wizard opens a refused connection in Upgrade security. Each problem is one plain sentence that names the setting or credential to fix.
Rules for every connector type:
insecure_skip_verify is refused. A cleartext address scheme is refused on every address setting, every Kafka bootstrap server, and every value in properties: http, ws, tcp, mqtt, rtsp, ftp, amqp and plaintext. Use https, wss, tls, mqtts, rtsps, ftps or amqps. An ssl_mode of disable, allow or prefer is refused. A Kafka security_protocol of plaintext or sasl_plaintext is refused. A connector type with no security rule cannot be used. Rules per connector type:
Type What it needs Kafka security_protocol sasl_ssl, sasl_mechanism scram-sha-512 or scram-sha-256, a username and a password credential. ssl alone is refused because it carries no login. The CA is optional (empty means the public roots). A Schema Registry, when set, is https with its own schema_registry_username and schema_registry_password. PostgreSQL, Redshift, MySQL ssl_mode stated as require, verify-ca or verify-full (unset is refused), a username and a password credential. MQTT A tls://, ssl://, mqtts:// or wss:// broker, use_tls on, a username and a password credential. RFID LLRP over TLS (use_tls, or llrps). The REST protocol needs an https endpoint. GPS telematics An https endpoint. The nmea provider is refused: it is a raw TCP stream with no encryption. Sensor gateway Modbus/TCP over TLS (use_tls, port 802), or an https endpoint. Object storage (S3, GCS, Azure) An https endpoint. A bare S3 host:port needs use_tls. Files The same as object storage, or an https SharePoint site_url. Salesforce, Guidewire, SAP, Dynamics 365, SharePoint, ServiceNow, logistics APIs, Flipper and Pineapple agents https addresses. A bare host that the connector would dial as http is refused. CCTV and video rtsps:// or https:// feeds. A device capture or a video file on the server dials nothing. Web pages https. A bare address is read as https. BigQuery, Snowflake, HubSpot, GitHub, Google Workspace, Databricks https by construction. An explicit http:// is refused. Excel, documents No network transport. A file path that is a URL must be https.
data.source-backing#Source backing:
source_backing states what stands behind a connection on this instance. It is computed from the connection’s address and dials nothing.
Value Meaning What it does not establish SOURCE_BACKING_LIVE Nothing that FACE ships stands in for this connection. Whatever it addresses is what it reads. That the source exists, is reachable, or works. A connection to a host that does not exist is still LIVE and simply fails. SOURCE_BACKING_UNSPECIFIED Not computed. Every RPC other than ListConnections leaves it unset. Anything about the connection. It is the absence of an answer, not a “live” one. When a connector fails, the failure is reported as a failure. FACE never substitutes other rows for a failed source. environment is not a substitute for this field: it is a free-form label for the tier of your estate a connection points at, such as “prod” or “staging”.
data.storage-and-replication#Storage and repl: Records are one replicated snapshot per tenant. FACE stores the snapshot in its own encrypted application filesystem and proposes changes through the platform’s consensus group, so every control-plane replica sees the same set of connections. Credential bundles are rows in the same encrypted store. Each row is sealed under a key derived for FACE and bound to its path. Bundles do not travel on the replication log. Only the record snapshot does. When a fetch runs on a dedicated runner, the control plane reads the bundle once (an audited read). It then seals the bundle to that runner’s in-memory key for that single dispatch. The runner never writes the credential to disk. See Runners. For the encryption and key model, see /docs/security/.
data.test-what-live_check_performed-means#Tes:
ConfigService.TestConnection resolves the connector for the connection’s type:
If the connector has a live probe, FACE runs it with the stored credentials. If the connector has no live probe, FACE says so and does not claim a result. Always read the two booleans together, never the message text:
success live_check_performed Meaning Typical message true true The connector dialled the source, and the source answered and accepted the credential. Connectivity verified true false The configuration is stored. Nothing was verified. The type has no live probe. Configuration saved — a live connectivity check isn't implemented yet for this source type false true The probe ran and failed. message is the connector’s own error. varies (see Troubleshooting) false false The connection could not be resolved. Connection not found, Unknown connection type "…", could not read the connection: … A successful probe establishes reachability and credential acceptance, and nothing more. It does not establish any of the following:
that a sensor is publishing that an antenna is attached that a probe is calibrated that the credential has scope for any other resource that any records exist Each connector page lists exactly what its probe does.
data.the-connection-record#The connection rec:
Connection (in face.proto) carries:
Field Meaning id Server-generated when empty (conn_). name Display name. It is never used to decide how a connection behaves. type The connector type, for example snowflake or mqtt. Matching ignores case, spaces, underscores and hyphens. environment Free-form tier label (prod, staging, …). It is not a statement about what stands behind the source. runner Which runner executes work for this connection. See Runners. config A oneof holding one typed configuration message, for example snowflake, mqtt or logistics_api. properties A map of extra non-secret settings. Many connectors read fallbacks from it. credential_state Filled by ListConnections (see below). source_backing Filled by ListConnections (see below).
data.where-you-add-and-choose-connections#Whe:
What you want Where Add, edit or remove a connection Settings › Integrations › Systems. New connection opens the connection wizard. A connection that an answer on Ask proposed opens there too, ready to confirm. Add, edit or remove a runner Settings › Integrations › Runners. See Runners. Choose the sources for a question Ask. Each connection is a card that reads Included in fetch or Not included. An admin can also switch a source Active or Inactive. An inactive source reads Switched off: not read by Fetch. Choose the sources for a brief Briefs, in the brief’s editor. Each run reads the connections ticked there. With all ticked, it reads every connection, including ones added later. A brief that reads nothing cannot be saved. Watch a live source The connection’s own card on Ask (see below). Live connection types have a view of their own. It opens from that connection’s card on Ask, with the connection already chosen:
Connection type Views on its card MQTT, sensor gateway, GPS telematics, RFID reader Live sensors, Devices CCTV, video stream, camera Surveillance Flipper Zero field reader Field reader, Devices A view opened from a card shows only that connection, with Show all to widen it.
The rest of this page is reference. A connection is made of two things that are stored apart: a record, which holds settings, and a credential bundle, which holds secrets. The sections below explain how they are split, stored and replicated, what the connection RPCs report, and the security every connection must meet.

data:
FACE learns about a source in three steps. Each step reads more than the one before it, and each is bounded separately.
Step RPC Reads Moves customer rows? Explore ConfigService.ExploreConnection The source’s own catalogue: dataset names, column names, declared types, nullability and declared constraints No Sample ConfigService.SampleConnectionDataset A bounded set of real rows from one dataset Yes, bounded Profile Used when FACE maps the estate, automatically at the start of a fetch A bounded row sample of named columns, plus optional per-column aggregates Bounded
data.explore#Explore:
Explore asks the connector to describe what the source holds, without assuming anything about its data model. The response is:
description (SourceDescription), which is never unset on a non-error return: supported: whether this source has a catalogue that FACE can read. reason: a human-readable explanation. Display it; do not match on it. datasets[]: each DescribedDataset has a name, a kind (table, view, entity set, topic, media track, …), a qualifier (for example DATABASE.SCHEMA or catalog.schema) and columns[], plus row counts, relationships, tags and partition keys where the source states them. datasets[].sample is always unset here, because Explore does not sample. aspects[]: which questions were asked (asked), whether the answer was readable (readable), the source call used (source), and a detail. Check this before concluding that something is absent. discovery_attempted: whether a connector’s discovery actually ran. It is false when the id did not resolve or the type has no connector. true together with supported=false is a normal, useful answer for a source with no catalogue. Every *_stated flag in the description means the source itself said so. A column’s nullable is meaningful only when nullable_stated is true, and the same rule applies to units, row counts, sizes and last-altered times. FACE never fills these in from defaults.
data.explore-support-by-connector#Explore sup: Connector Explore reads PostgreSQL, MySQL information_schema tables and columns, up to 500 tables. Declared primary, unique and foreign keys come from pg_catalog.pg_constraint on PostgreSQL and information_schema on MySQL. PostgreSQL (also) Table, view and column comments from pg_catalog.pg_description, and view definitions from pg_get_viewdef, for the listed datasets. Partitions and extension-owned relations are not listed, and the count left out is stated. Reading them needs no role beyond the default PUBLIC access to pg_catalog. Snowflake INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES and .COLUMNS for the connection’s database (and schema, when set), including ROW_COUNT where Snowflake maintains it. Databricks system.information_schema columns and tables, column tags (declared units and PII classes), and CHECK … IN (…) vocabularies. It is metastore-wide unless a catalog property scopes it. SAP (OData) One GET of the service $metadata (CSDL). Entity sets become datasets. Salesforce Org version list, Describe Global, then a per-object describe (up to 200 objects described). Guidewire /rest/apis, the per-API OpenAPI documents and typelists. Kafka Topic catalogue (Metadata) plus Schema Registry value schemas. It reads no record. CCTV RTSP DESCRIBE, or ONVIF profiles followed by DESCRIBE. Flipper edge reader The edge agent’s capability catalogue. All others supported=false with a reason that says whether the source has no catalogue at all (Modbus, device capture, a file) or the connector does not read one.
data.profile#Profile:
FACE maps the estate as part of every fetch, over the connections that fetch reads; a newly confirmed connection joins at the next fetch. There is no separate control to map it by hand. When it maps the estate for analysis, it profiles each connection within fixed budgets:
Which datasets. At most 12 datasets per connection are profiled, taken in catalogue order. The result reports datasets_profiled next to datasets_discovered.
Sample reads. FACE reads the columns it names from the catalogue. It never uses SELECT * and adds no COUNT(*). The default is 25 rows, with ceilings of 100 rows, 64 columns and 512 bytes per value.
Time. The deadline is 30 s by default and at most 2 minutes. The deadline bounds how long FACE waits, not the work the warehouse does.
Statistics. An optional aggregate pass computes, per column:
non-null and null counts null rate distinct count range (min/max) mean and standard deviation Each figure carries a *Stated flag and a basis. A range can be withheld with a stated reason.
Opting out. A connection listed in metadata_only_connection_ids is read for its catalogue only, and no data is read.
No sampled value is ever written to a log.
data.sample#Sample:
SampleConnectionDataset is the one ConfigService RPC that moves customer data. You name one dataset by qualifier and name, exactly as Explore reported them. The server re-quotes both parts for each engine. Every identifier part goes through an identifier allowlist first, and a name that the allowlist rejects is refused with the reason. It is never escaped or quoted around.
Bounds:
row_limit must be in 0..1000. 0 means the connector’s default. A value outside that range is refused, not clamped.
Each connector applies its own ceiling:
Connector Default rows Ceiling Cell size cap Method Snowflake 10 100 512 bytes FIXED_SIZE_RANDOM (SAMPLE (n ROWS)) Databricks 25 1000 (above is refused) 4096 bytes FIRST_ROWS (the first rows the engine produced) Sampling is served for the connectors in the table above. Any other type answers sampled: false with a reason naming the source type. Use Explore for its structure.
Before sampling, the server explores the dataset to learn its governance (masked columns, row filters). The response sample then carries:
columns and rows. Each SampleCell separates is_null from an empty value. method and method_detail: the statistical class and the source’s own clause. masked_columns, row_filter and governance_checked. governance_checked is false when the governance answer could not be obtained. caveats, which is never empty. Show masked_columns, row_filter and governance_checked beside the rows. A masked column returns its masked value and still counts as a successful read.
Sampled rows are not the dataset. A null rate, a distinct count or an absent value computed over 25 rows says nothing about the table.
data.which-values-may-leave-a-source-during-e:
Explore reads metadata only. It does not read:
row counts that would need a scan (COUNT(*)) most-common-value lists or histograms, because those are literal customer values sample rows A catalogue is permission-filtered. What comes back is what this credential can see, which may be smaller than what exists.

data:
The Flipper connector reads a handheld field reader: a Flipper Zero that an operator carries on a yard walk, a dock inspection or a cold-store sweep. It covers the places fixed telemetry does not reach, such as a third-party crossdock, a trailer from a carrier who shares no feed, or an uninstrumented freezer room.
You add the reader in Settings › Integrations › Systems. Its card on Ask then opens Field reader, the live view, and Devices, the devices it reported, with that reader already chosen.
Readings from a handheld are sparse and hand-initiated. A gap between two readings means nobody was standing there, not that a feed dropped. FACE states a cadence only when a sweep was configured with one.
data.behaviour#Behaviour: Test calls the agent’s /healthz and succeeds only when the agent reports a connected device. Otherwise the message says which layer failed: the agent is running with no device, or the link is open but the device does not answer RPC. Execute calls /readings with the sweep context. It returns SensorReading rows exactly as the agent reported them. Responses are capped at 1 MiB. An agent answer with success: false is passed through as a failure. Explore reads the agent’s /capabilities catalogue.
data.how-it-connects#How it connects:
FACE does not talk to the device directly. It makes HTTPS requests to the edge device agent (flipperd), which runs next to the Flipper and owns its serial or USB link. Replugs, flat batteries and reboots are handled locally by the agent.
Type spellings flipper, flipperzero, handheld, fieldreader Settings (properties) agent_url (also endpoint, url, base_url, host): the agent’s https:// address. http:// is refused, and so is an address with no scheme, which the connector would dial as http. Sweep context (properties, passed to the agent) reader_id (device_id, reader), location (site), reference (shipment_reference), carrier, threshold_source, threshold_min, threshold_max, max_excursion_minutes Credential token (also api_key, agent_token), sent as Authorization: Bearer Internal addresses Controlled per connection with allow_internal_network (the agent is usually on a local network)
data.what-it-will-not-fabricate#What it will: A Flipper Zero has no cargo thermometer. Its only onboard temperature is the battery fuel gauge inside its own case. The agent reports that value as reader_enclosure_temperature, and FACE never renames, rescales or reinterprets a metric. A reading that measures the reader keeps saying so. Thresholds and their *_stated flags are copied verbatim from what the operator stated for the sweep.

data: The SaaS and ERP connectors speak each vendor’s REST or OData API directly. Each section below lists what the connector reads, the settings it takes and what Test checks.
data.google-workspace#Google Workspace:
Google Workspace is read only during a fetch, through two connection types. Test and Explore apply to registry connectors, so Test reports Unknown connection type for these two types. Google Docs is not a connection type: FACE does not read Google Docs.
Type What a fetch reads Settings gmail Up to 5 messages matching the fetch command as a Gmail query (label:INBOX when the command is fetch) — google_sheets One range of one spreadsheet properties spreadsheet_id (falls back to the connection name) and range (default A1:Z50) Credentials: google_service_account_json. Without it, the instance-wide Google integration configured in Settings › Integrations › Channels is used. The type is matched case-insensitively but otherwise exactly (google_sheets, not Google Sheets).
data.guidewire#Guidewire: Config message GuidewireConnectionConfig: base_url (the Cloud API root), tenant_id Credentials username and password, sent as HTTP Basic Properties resource (also route, path): the route a fetch reads. max_records / max_rows. Internal addresses Controlled per connection with allow_internal_network Test calls /rest/apis and requires a non-empty API list. Extraction reads one resource (the query or resource) inside the base_url path. A route that escapes the base path is refused. Page size: 200 by default, 500 maximum. Rows: 5,000 by default, 50,000 maximum. Paging: at most 200 pages within 3 minutes. links.next is followed on the same host only. A 200 response without Guidewire’s data envelope is refused rather than read as empty. Explore enumerates /rest/apis, the per-API OpenAPI documents and the typelists. Typelist vocabularies are marked complete when the codes served match the count the index declares. The connector speaks HTTP Basic, which is what self-managed installations use.
data.salesforce#Salesforce: Config message SalesforceConnectionConfig: login_url, client_id Credentials username, password, security_token (appended to the password), client_secret Auth OAuth 2.0 username–password flow against /services/oauth2/token Properties soql (the query a fetch runs), api_version (default v60.0; must match vNN.N), max_records / max_rows, include_deleted (uses queryAll) Internal addresses Controlled per connection with allow_internal_network Test posts the token request to the login host. A success means the credentials were accepted. Discovery and queries then dial the instance_url that the token response names. Extraction runs one SOQL statement, either the query you pass or the connection’s soql property. The connector does not choose objects for you. It follows nextRecordsUrl on the same host only. Rows: default 5,000, at most 50,000. Paging: at most 200 pages within a 3-minute budget. A response that contradicts itself (done with a next page, or not done without one) is refused rather than returned short. Explore reads the org’s version list, then Describe Global, then a describe per object: Up to 200 objects get column detail. The rest are listed without columns, and the reason says how many. Picklists become vocabularies (up to 512 values). A vocabulary is marked complete only when the org flags the picklist as restricted. Lookup targets appear in the declared type as reference(Account). No row counts are requested, to protect your metered API allocation.
data.sap-odata--csdl#SAP (OData / CSDL):
SAP connections describe an SAP system through SAPConnectionConfig (system_id, client, username, password, host, system_number). Those are RFC and SAP GUI destination parameters. OData discovery is driven by connection properties:
Property Meaning odata_url (also odata_base_url, odata_service_url, service_url, base_url, endpoint, url) The OData service root. Write it as https://…: http:// is refused, and the connector would dial a value with no scheme as http. The URL must not contain user:pass@. odata_service_path (also service_path, service) Appended to the service root sap_client (also sap-client, mandt, client) Sent as the sap-client query parameter sap_gateway_url Instead of one service: the Gateway origin, whose OData V2 service catalogue is enumerated Credentials: username (setting or credential), and password (also api_key, token or secret) from the credential bundle. Internal addresses are allowed by default, because SAP systems usually live on private networks.
Explore. One GET of the service’s $metadata, capped at 16 MiB. Entity sets become datasets of kind entityset, qualified by the CSDL namespace. Properties keep their document order and the service’s own type spelling (for example Edm.Decimal(13,3)). Literal units come from Measures.Unit / ISOCurrency, and PII flags from PersonalData.IsPotentiallyPersonal. Validation.AllowedValues becomes a vocabulary (up to 128 values). It is always reported as incomplete, because CSDL does not enforce it. Nullability is reported only where the document states it. No row counts are requested. Test. Saves the configuration. Explore is the reachability check: it reads the service’s $metadata.
data.servicenow#ServiceNow:
ServiceNow settings are read from connection properties: systemUrl (the instance URL). The credentials are username and password (HTTP Basic). Internal addresses are refused unless allow_internal_network=true is set.
Extraction reads the Table API tables syslog, sysevent and sys_audit, with an 8 MiB cap per response. Test requests the first of those tables. Explore returns supported=false. ServiceNow data is read through extraction.
data.summary#Summary:
Connector Type spellings Test Explore Extraction SAP (OData) sap No live probe Yes ($metadata) Metadata through Explore Salesforce salesforce Live (OAuth token request) Yes SOQL query with paging Guidewire guidewire Live (/rest/apis) Yes Cloud API resource reads with paging ServiceNow servicenow Live (Table API request) No catalogue read Fixed Table API tables Google Workspace gmail, google_sheets (fetch only) Not available No Gmail and Sheets reads during a fetch For a type with no live probe, Test returns success: true with live_check_performed: false, which means the configuration was saved and nothing was verified. See Connections and credentials.
Every address on these connectors must be https://. http:// is refused, and so is a bare host that the connector would dial as http (SAP’s host and base_url, Guidewire’s base_url). A bare ServiceNow instance name and an empty Salesforce login_url are dialled as https. See Security requirements.
All HTTP-based connectors here dial through FACE’s hardened HTTP client. It uses no proxy, applies the address policy, and follows at most 5 redirects, all to the same host. A redirect to a different host is refused, so a credential never travels to a host the connection did not name.

data:
A data listener follows one connection’s stream of business changes: rows changed in a transactional database, records produced to a Kafka topic. It counts them, meters them, and hands them to briefs that run when data changes, which run a fetch when the changes you ask for arrive.
The listener itself reads only each change’s coordinates (where, what kind, which key), never its values. The run it fires is a fetch like any other: it reads the connection’s tables with the connection’s own login, reads back the rows that changed, and reports which business rules those rows conform to or break. Nothing is installed in your source by FACE.
It is not the Metadata listener on a connection in Settings › Integrations › Systems, which watches a source for schema changes. The two are switched on separately.
data.apache-kafka#Apache Kafka: Nothing to install. The listener reads the connection’s topics (its Topics prefix filter, or every non-internal topic) without a consumer group, so it never moves an offset your own consumers depend on. It starts at each partition’s latest offset: it reports what is produced while it runs, not the topic’s history. A Kafka event carries its topic and record key; there is no row to read back, so the run’s rule results cite record keys.
data.check-the-connection#Check the connectio: In Settings › Integrations › Systems, the PostgreSQL connection must test green with the login that will read it, and the ledger must be installed (above). A Kafka connection needs nothing more. Both must meet the security requirements.
data.choose-when-data-changes#Choose When dat: Under When, select When data changes. The time options give way to the event settings.
data.metering#Metering:
A listener’s usage is recorded in FACE’s usage ledger, against the purchaser of the person who created the brief that switched it on:
Metric Quantity listener_events events read listener_seconds seconds spent listening Each record is written once: a repeated report or a restarted control plane never records the same usage twice. Someone not placed on a purchaser’s account is metered to the platform account, and Briefs says so next to Metered to. The bytes read are shown on Briefs and are not a billed metric. The fetch an event fires is metered as any fetch is.
These two metrics are recorded and shown; how they are priced on a bill is set by your plan.
data.open-a-new-brief#Open a new brief: Open Briefs under Fetch in the rail and select CREATE NEW SCHEDULE. The editor is titled New brief. Under What to ask, type the question each run asks, for example one about freight billing, or pick one under Start from a common question.
data.postgresql-the-change-event-ledger#Postg:
The listener needs your database to say what changed. It uses an ordinary trigger, a ledger table and NOTIFY, not logical replication:
Logical replication needs wal_level=logical, a role with REPLICATION that streams every column of every published table, and a replication slot. A slot whose consumer is away keeps WAL without limit, which can fill the database’s disk. The ledger costs one small row per change and keeps least privilege: the connection’s login only needs SELECT on one more table. NOTIFY is only a wake-up call; a listener that was disconnected reads every row after the last one it saw, so nothing is lost. Your database administrator runs this once, adapting the table list to yours. Each trigger names its table’s business-key column; the ledger records the schema-qualified table and that column, so an event-fired run can read the changed row back. Grant the connection’s login SELECT on the ledger and on the tables it reads.
CREATE TABLE ops.change_events ( seq bigserial PRIMARY KEY, occurred_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp(), table_name text NOT NULL, -- schema.table op text NOT NULL CHECK (op IN ('INSERT', 'UPDATE', 'DELETE')), key_column text NOT NULL, row_key text NOT NULL, provenance text NOT NULL DEFAULT '' ); -- TG_ARGV[0] names the table's business-key column. CREATE FUNCTION ops.record_change() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ DECLARE k text; s bigint; BEGIN IF TG_OP = 'DELETE' THEN k := to_jsonb(OLD) ->> TG_ARGV[0]; ELSE k := to_jsonb(NEW) ->> TG_ARGV[0]; END IF; INSERT INTO ops.change_events (table_name, op, key_column, row_key) VALUES (TG_TABLE_SCHEMA || '.' || TG_TABLE_NAME, TG_OP, TG_ARGV[0], COALESCE(k, '')) RETURNING seq INTO s; PERFORM pg_notify('face_ops_events', s::text); RETURN NULL; END; $$; CREATE TRIGGER shipments_change AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON ops.shipments FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION ops.record_change('shipment_id'); GRANT SELECT ON ops.change_events TO face_reader; Table and column names must be lower case. The listener reads ops.change_events and listens on face_ops_events by default. To use other names, set two properties on the connection: face.events.ledger (schema.table, lower case) and face.events.channel. The ledger grows by one row per change, so delete old rows on your own schedule; the listener only reads rows newer than the last one it saw.
data.read-what-the-run-found#Read what the ru: When matching events arrive, the card’s LAST TRIGGER shows how many events fired the run and the first five of them (table or topic, operation, key), how many of their rows were read back, the run’s transaction id and its outcome. When the run’s analysis finishes, a few minutes later, RULE RESULTS FROM THESE CHANGES lists each rule the triggering rows bear on: its verdict (Drift, Shadow, Missing or Aligned), its id and category, and Rows: the keys of the rows it is about. The same rules appear among the business rules on Why.
data.save#Save: Select Save brief. On Briefs, its card shows the EVENT chip beside ACTIVE, and NEXT RUN reads On the next matching event.
data.say-which-changes-count#Say which change:
Listen to: the PostgreSQL or Kafka connection. Only those types are listed. Run after this many events: for example 1 to analyse every change, or 5 for a batch. Wait for more events (seconds): so a burst of changes becomes one run. At most one run every (minutes): the cooldown; never less than one minute. Only tables or topics starting with: for example ops.freight_invoices; empty means all. Only this change: for example INSERT; Any change means all. The note under these settings says what saving does: it turns the connection’s data listener on, on the managed runner, and installs nothing.
Under Where to look, tick the connections each run reads.
data.set-up-an-event-triggered-analysis#Set u: The listener has one switch: the briefs that run when its data changes. Saving an active brief of that kind turns the connection’s listener on; pausing or deleting the last one on that connection turns it off.
data.the-validation-estate#The validation est:
Runink’s own validation cluster runs the quickstart PostgreSQL with this ledger installed, three more operational tables, and a transactional writer that keeps the quickstart estate moving. Every row the writer produces carries its own ids (SO-9…, SHP-9…, SINV-9…, CLM-9…) and a provenance column naming the quickstart estate.
Table Rule its rows exercise How often the writer breaks it ops.freight_invoices billed rate per mile equals the carrier’s contract rate (the MySQL estate’s freight.rate_contracts) about 12% of invoices bill 8–18% over ops.shipments delivered by the planned time about 15% of deliveries are late ops.claims filed within the contract’s claim window (60, 90 or 120 days) about 15% of claims are filed on a July 2026 shipment, past its window ops.inventory_positions on hand stays above the reorder point order lines draw stock down and restocking lags, so a position sits below it for a while Every 20 seconds the writer creates orders and their lines, ships, delivers and invoices shipments, files claims and restocks low positions; most rows conform. A brief that runs when data changes, asking about freight billing, filtered to ops.freight_invoices and INSERT, has an off-contract invoice to find within minutes.
data.watch-the-listener#Watch the listener: DATA LISTENERS heads the Briefs page, one row per connection: the state the runner last reported (LISTENING, STARTING, DEGRADED, NOT LISTENING with the reason, or OFF), how it reads, the events and bytes it read, how long it has listened, and Metered to. Within about 15 seconds of saving, the row reads LISTENING.
data.what-an-event-fired-run-reports#What an:
A brief that runs when data changes fires a fetch with the events that fired it (the first and the newest, at most 25) and the connection that saw them. The runner reads back the rows those events name, at most 50, with the connection’s own login: a parameterised SELECT by key on each table, and a key whose row is gone (deleted, or pruned since) is reported as gone, never guessed. The analysis receives them as the changes that triggered the run and gives each rule it finds the keys of the triggering rows it is about.
Only keys that really fired the run are kept: a key the analysis cites that was not a triggering row is dropped, and a rule that cites none is not attributed to the run. Each result is shown with the rows it rests on, so you can check it against the source. An event-fired run never reuses an earlier answer to the same question: its subject is the rows that fired it.
data.which-sources#Which sources: Source How it listens What you install PostgreSQL LISTEN on a channel, then reads a change-event ledger table the ledger, once, by your DBA (below) Apache Kafka reads every partition of the connection’s topics from the latest offsets nothing Other source types have no data listener. A connection bound to a self-hosted runner is reported NOT LISTENING with that reason: listening runs on the managed runner only, and a connection bound to a runner is never moved to another one.

data: FACE reads spreadsheets, delimited and JSON files, Parquet, and objects in your own cloud buckets. Every read is streamed and bounded, and a clipped read is always marked as truncated.
data.document-sources#Document sources:
A fetch hands the following connection types to FACE’s document extraction (OCR) path rather than to a tabular connector:
gdrive gcp_bucket sftp local pdf word network They read connection properties: path (it falls back to the connection name), host, port, and bucket for buckets. Their output is extracted text.
SFTP requires a verified host key and refuses to connect without one. Downloads stop if nothing arrives for 60 seconds. Downloads are capped at 2 GiB by default. The operator setting FACE_MAX_DOWNLOAD_BYTES changes the cap. These types have no registry connector, so Test and Explore do not apply to them.
Of these types, only sftp meets the connector security policy. The others have no security rule, so a connection of those types cannot be saved, and a stored one is refused when a fetch reads it.
data.excel#Excel: Type spellings excel, xlsx, spreadsheet Config message ExcelConnectionConfig: file_path, has_header Credentials None (CREDENTIAL_STATE_NONE_NEEDED) Test Checks that file_path exists on the reading node, is not a directory, and ends in .xlsx or .xlsm. It is a local file check, not a network dial. Execute Reads one sheet. The query names the sheet, and an empty query reads the first sheet. Rows are decoded one at a time and stop at the row cap. Explore supported=false. A workbook’s sheets and header row are its schema. For CSV and other delimited text, use an object-store connection or a document source.
data.object-storage-s3-gcs-azure-blob#Object:
Type spellings objectstore, s3, awss3, gcs, googlecloudstorage, azureblob, azure, blobstorage Config message ObjectStoreConnectionConfig Setting Meaning provider s3, gcs or azure. Aliases such as minio, ceph, aws, gcp and azblob are normalised. It is required, and an unknown provider is refused. bucket The bucket, or the container for Azure. Required. prefix An optional key prefix that scopes the connection region S3 region endpoint An S3-compatible endpoint (MinIO, Ceph, your own objectd). Empty means AWS S3 over TLS. For GCS or Azure, a custom service endpoint. It must be https://: http:// is refused. account Azure storage account name (required for Azure) use_tls Whether an S3-compatible endpoint given without a scheme uses TLS. A scheme on endpoint overrides it. A bare S3 host:port without use_tls is refused. Credential keys:
Provider Keys S3 access_key and secret_key (also aws_access_key_id / aws_secret_access_key), optional session_token GCS service_account_json (also credentials_json, google_credentials). It may be omitted only with a custom endpoint. Azure account_key, or sas_token, or connection_string Test has a 10-second budget and runs one live call per provider: S3 BucketExists, GCS bucket attributes, or Azure container properties. Messages distinguish “does not exist, or these credentials cannot see it” from “cannot reach”. Execute reads one object. The query is the object key, and prefix is prepended when the key does not already start with it. Parquet objects are read from their footer, and all other formats are streamed. Object reads use S3-compatible stores; for GCS and Azure, Test checks the bucket or container. Explore returns supported=false. Listing a bucket gives keys, not a schema.
data.parquet#Parquet: A Parquet file is read from its footer, so FACE needs its size and random access. That makes an object in an S3-compatible store the supported source. FACE reads in batches of 256 rows under the same row cap. A file larger than the byte ceiling is refused with parquet file is … bytes, beyond the …-byte ceiling.
data.read-bounds-all-file-formats#Read bounds:
Bound Default Meaning Bytes read 64 MiB A ceiling on what is read from the source, including a single pathological line Rows kept 10,000 A ceiling on what is returned When either bound is reached, the response message ends with — TRUNCATED: .
Supported formats: csv, tsv, json (a top-level array), jsonl / ndjson, txt, html, parquet, and xlsx / xlsm for Excel. For objects, FACE takes the format from the key’s extension.

data: Order, transport, warehouse, yard and inventory management systems are read by one REST implementation, parameterised by system. Across these systems, what differs is the default resource and the vendor’s paging and filter dialect. Those differences are data, not separate connectors.
data.behaviour#Behaviour: Test requests the target resource with a page size of 1, within 15 s. A success means the API answered and accepted the credential. Execute pages through the resource: Within the record cap, at most 200 pages, and a 3-minute budget. Each page is capped at 16 MiB. Redirects are followed on the same host only, up to 5. Rows are the records as the API returns them. The columns are the union of fields seen across the rows. An empty result is reported as Success=false: connector reached … and received no records. Explore returns supported=false. These systems publish no common catalogue. Internal addresses. Set allow_internal_network to control whether the connection may reach internal addresses.
data.credentials-by-auth_mode#Credentials by: auth_mode Credential keys api_key api_key (also apikey, token, access_token), sent in api_key_header bearer token (also bearer_token, access_token, api_key) basic username and password oauth2_client_credentials client_id and client_secret. The token is cached until shortly before it expires. none —

Setting provider changes the paging and changed-since parameters:

Setting Meaning system oms, wms, whs, yms, tms, ims (and the other systems above) provider The vendor dialect (see above) base_url An https:// URL. Required. http:// is refused, and so is a value with no scheme, which the connector would dial as http. resource The resource path to read. The default paging parameters are limit, offset and cursor.

data.allowing-internal-addresses-on-a-connect:
A connection whose source genuinely sits inside your network, such as a reader or gateway on the plant network, can be allowed to reach internal addresses with the property allow_internal_network (also accepted: allow_private_network, allow_internal). Use true or false. When an address is refused, the message names the property:
refusing to reach 10.1.2.3: it resolves to a private address, which is inside this deployment's own network rather than on the public internet. If that is genuinely the source you mean, set `allow_internal_network=true` on this connection
data.connector-address-policy#Connector addre: Connectors dial addresses that people type into a form. To stop those addresses from reaching the platform’s own internals, outbound connections are checked against an egress policy on the address actually being connected to, after DNS resolution. The policy blocks internal and cloud metadata addresses unless an operator explicitly allows a connection to reach internal addresses; the cloud instance-metadata service is never a data source.
data.ipv6-first-ipv4-fully-supported#IPv6 fir:
The Runink platform is IPv6-first, and many data platforms are still reachable only over IPv4. FACE supports both, so no connector pins an address family.
TCP dials use Happy Eyeballs (RFC 8305). This covers the HTTP-based connectors, the raw-socket protocols (MQTT, LLRP, Modbus, NMEA, Kafka, RTSP), the Snowflake and Databricks transports, and the PostgreSQL and MySQL drivers. When a name resolves to both IPv6 and IPv4 addresses, FACE races them and uses whichever connects first. gRPC dials (control plane to runner) try addresses in order. They follow RFC 6724 preference, so IPv6 comes first, and fall back to the next address after a connect timeout. They do not race. Reaching IPv4-only services from an IPv6-only network needs NAT64 or an equivalent egress path. That is a deployment concern, not a connector setting. See /docs/operations/.
data.redirects-and-proxies#Redirects and prox: Redirects. HTTP connectors follow redirects only to the same host. A redirect to another host is refused, so a credential sent to the source you named is never replayed to a different one: refusing to follow a redirect from … to …. Proxies. Connector HTTP clients use no proxy, so the address that is checked is the address that is connected to.
data.timeouts-and-body-caps#Timeouts and body:
Every connector bounds its dial, its handshake and its response body. Over-cap responses are refused rather than read short. See each connector page for its figures. When a body exceeds its cap, the message is:
… returned more than N bytes: refusing to report a partially-read answer as a complete one — narrow the request (a shorter collection window, a smaller page size, a single resource) or point the connection at an endpoint that pages
data.writing-addresses#Writing addresses:
IPv6 literals need brackets when a port is given: [2001:db8::10]:5432, rtsps://[2001:db8::20]:322/stream, tls://[2001:db8::30]:8883.
A bare IPv6 literal without a port is also accepted where a connector applies a default port. FACE detects “has a port” by parsing, not by looking for a colon, so 2001:db8::10 gets the default port appended and bracketed correctly.
Default ports:
Protocol Default port PostgreSQL 5432 MySQL 3306 MQTT over TLS 8883 LLRP 5084 Modbus-TCP over TLS 802 Kafka 9092 RTSPS state the port in the URL Databricks 443 Runner https:// endpoint 443 Every address must use an encrypted transport. Cleartext schemes such as http://, tcp://, mqtt:// and rtsp:// are refused. See Security requirements.
A URL must not contain credentials (user:pass@). Connectors that parse URLs refuse them and ask you to store the credential on the connection instead.

data:
The test-estate safety rule: stand the test estate up only beside a test instance, never a production deployment. Its systems are throwaway test services with published credentials: change-me is every test credential. They are still encrypted and still ask for a login, because FACE refuses a connection that is not (see Connector security). Use a scratch machine or a scratch cluster. Runink FACE: Fulfilment Autonomous Claims Engine connects to the systems a logistics team already runs. These quickstarts give every one of the 32 connection types in the catalogue the quickstart estate, a real dataset you can download, load and fetch: one company, Quillmere Freight Lines, written out in each system’s native shape, with the model FACE should find in it.
Start with See all connectors at once: it is the walkthrough across every source, and it shows where the evidence for each of the six planted anomalies lives.
data.connector-security#Connector security:
FACE refuses a connection that would send data, or the login that reads it, unencrypted. It refuses it when you save it, and it refuses again on every read of a stored connection that does not meet the rule. The error names each setting to fix and says to open the connection in Settings › Integrations and upgrade its security. The rule holds for the test estate too, so every test connection on these pages is the secured form.
For every type:
insecure_skip_verify must be off: the server’s certificate is always checked. No address may use a cleartext scheme: http, ws, tcp, mqtt, rtsp, ftp, amqp or plaintext. Use https, wss, tls, mqtts, rtsps, ftps or amqps. ssl_mode may not be disable, allow or prefer, and a Kafka security_protocol may not be plaintext or sasl_plaintext. What each type needs on top of that:
Type Needs Kafka security_protocol sasl_ssl; sasl_mechanism scram-sha-512 or scram-sha-256; a username and the password credential. A Schema Registry, when named, is https:// with its own schema_registry_username and schema_registry_password. ssl_ca_pem is optional. PostgreSQL, Redshift, MySQL ssl_mode stated as require, verify-ca or verify-full (unset is refused); a username and the password credential. MQTT, IoT A tls://, ssl://, mqtts:// or wss:// broker, use_tls on, a username and the password credential. RFID LLRP over TLS (use_tls on, or llrps). A reader read over HTTP must use https://. GPS An https:// endpoint. Provider nmea is a raw TCP stream with no encryption and is refused. Sensor gateway Modbus/TCP over TLS (use_tls on, port 802), or an https:// endpoint. Object store, files An https:// endpoint, or use_tls on for a bare S3 host. CCTV An rtsps:// or https:// feed. rtsp:// and http:// are refused. Logistics systems, SAP, Guidewire, field readers https:// addresses. A bare host is refused, because FACE would dial it unencrypted. Salesforce, ServiceNow, Dynamics 365, SharePoint, web pages https:// addresses. A bare host is read as https. BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, HubSpot, GitHub Nothing more: their APIs are https by construction. Excel, Document Nothing more: nothing is dialled. An Excel file_path that is a URL must be https://. A type FACE has no security rule for cannot be used.
data.downloads#Downloads:
There are 25 zips for 32 connection types, and none is missing. The 7 streaming connectors (cctv, gps, iot, kafka, mqtt, rfid and sensorgateway) are dialled and held open, so they ship as replayable stream recordings under streams//, not as zips. The other 25 types each have one zip.
The downloads live at https://docs.runink.org/downloads/connections/, keyed by connection type, so every Runink product’s docs link to the same files. Every download is generated at publish time, from a fixed seed, and scanned before it is published: hosts end in .invalid, addresses are in the documentation ranges, and the only credential value is change-me.
universe.json: the reconciliation graph. Every shared entity, every link between sources, and the six planted anomalies with their evidence. manifest.json: every download with its size and SHA-256. SHA256SUMS: the same list, for sha256sum -c.

Grade each type honestly before you pick one to try.

There is no vendor system to stand up for this type; load the dataset and fetch it. Every one of the 32 has a quickstart dataset and an expected model, whatever its grade.
