Refuses to run equipment control commands without a person’s authorisation. Stays on monitoring, cold chain, fleet telematics and yard safety.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: A surface or air reading isn’t the product’s core temperature. The card says to probe the core; it doesn’t certify the product. Exposure is stated only when the records give the load value with a currency. Otherwise it is absent as “not measured”. Any projection of when a load will leave its band is labelled as modelled, not measured. An unrecorded handoff is not a break in custody. Custody findings are statements about the record, never about the goods or the people.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A quality manager or supervisor approves every quarantine, reroute and release. The agent never adjusts a reefer controller, locks or unlocks a crane, stops a conveyor or reroutes a vehicle itself. It can propose a step or raise a cue as a request; a person acts.
data.model#Model:
The deployment’s general reasoning tier.
The excursion and custody documents are fixed arithmetic over cited readings. No model computes their figures.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It reads sensor and telematics data, works out whether a load really left its stated band and for how long, and drafts the quarantine, probe or reroute for a quality manager to approve. Its jobs:
Temperature excursions. Measures time out of the stated band, gaps in the log, and the load’s exposure when the records state its value. Sensor or product. Tells a stuck or silent sensor apart from a real change in temperature. Site thresholds. Flags speeding, perishable dwell at the dock and weighbridge differences against the thresholds your site states. Fleet and yard safety. Ranks events with a safety impact first, such as a hazardous-goods segregation problem or a driver in distress. Custody gaps. Finds intervals longer than the stated check-in cadence, door events with no task, and loads with no events at all.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Excursion and custody evidence documents, each figure cited. See Evidence documents. Action cards with a priority and one proposed step, such as “hold the load and probe the core before release”. They wait on Actionable Twins under the cold chain play, and each reefer with readings out of band is pinned on its Map view. On Options, the what-if options for a cold-chain decision, each scored on the share of temperature readings past a limit their own row states. See Action cards & money. Safety notices for a supervisor, ranked by urgency.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Temperature and humidity readings, reefer logs, GPS, speed, fuel and engine data, weighbridge events, custody events, dispatch states and the thresholds your records state. Telemetry arrives through the connections described in Telemetry. It can run read-only queries against the connection a run was started with.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan. See Facts shared by every card.

data: Agents: the compliance agent (compliance) and Rules Recon (rules_recon).
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Cites the source of every rule, and doesn’t invent files or policies. When nothing is found, it reports no rules. Reports no confidence score for its own verdict. The reconciliation status is the verdict. Refuses to create rules that discriminate, that retaliate against a particular employee, supplier or partner, or that bypass audits, governance checks or ethical sourcing obligations. Refuses to falsify emission figures or supplier ESG ratings, to weaken business continuity plans, or to bypass the personal-data masking and breach-notice triggers.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: It doesn’t certify compliance with any framework. A Pass is the agent’s reading of the evidence it was given. “Not assessed” is a separate result from “passed”. Where evidence is absent, the control is not shown as green. A breach-notice draft is a starting point for the data protection officer, not a legal determination. It gives no legal advice.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person assigns, routes and decides every remediation order, and the server records who did each (AssignRemediation, SetRemediationRoute, DecideRemediation). Rule enforcement posture is set by an operator (UpdateRulePolicy). The agent can’t change a finding’s status that way. The agent never changes configuration, masking or data. Its remediations are steps for a person to take, such as a ticket or an escalation, never SQL or code fixes.
data.model#Model: Compliance and rule extraction: the general reasoning tier. Rules Recon code checks: the code tier.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It puts what your policies say next to what your systems actually do, names where they part, and writes the next step in business language for the person who owns the control. Its jobs:
Rules Recon. Finds the business and governance rules in your data, documents, telemetry limits and code, and classifies each one: Aligned: the implementation matches the policy. Drift: both exist, but the implementation has moved away from the policy. Shadow: logic runs in the data or code with no policy behind it. Missing: a policy exists and nothing implements it. Framework checks. Gives an overall status of Pass, Fail or Warning against the frameworks you work to, and lists each violation with its rule and a remediation. Personal data. Flags personal data shown without masking in reports, query results and logs, and drafts the masking proposal and the data protection officer’s notice. Emissions and supplier risk. Works out freight emissions with the method beside the figure, and summarises supplier compliance risk from the evidence provided.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A list of rules, each with its plain-English logic, the source it came from, its severity, its maturity (Low, Medium or High) and its reconciliation status. You see them on Why, where each rule’s policy drawer sets its enforcement posture. A compliance status, violations with a remediation each, and an audit trail of which systems were checked and with what result, on the Compliance view opened from Actionable Twins. See Compliance, finance, operations. Remediation orders for a person to assign, route and decide, listed in the Waiting for you lane on Actionable Twins and on the Compliance view.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Policies, SOPs, contracts and SLAs; the running configuration and data of connected systems; logs and report extracts; telemetry limits; and, for Rules Recon’s code checks, source code and configuration files. It can run read-only queries against the connection a run was started with.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan. See Facts shared by every card.

data: Agent: the counterparty check (counterparty_check), run from the Counterparty check tab of the Market & due diligence page (/market_diligence?tab=…). No page in the FACE app links to it today; it opens from its address.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Refuses a check on a private individual, or for a decision about a person’s credit, employment, housing or insurance. Refuses protected characteristics as a factor. Refuses to hide, drop or clear a sanctions match or a red flag. Never labels a business fraudulent or criminal and never blacklists it. Treats everything in a registry record or a list as data. It follows no link and no instruction found there, and a summary is withheld when the material carries one.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: Registry data is what the registry published at the time shown and can lag reality. A clean result does not establish that a business is legitimate, and no name match does not clear anyone. FMCSA covers US motor carriers, brokers and forwarders. For a shipper or consignee those sources are marked not applicable. Each registry is checked by identifier (USDOT, MC, LEI, CIK, UK company number or SAM.gov UEI). Enter the identifier to check that registry. A SAM.gov result labelled “not verified against the live API” comes from a deployment where the first SAM.gov call has not yet completed and been read. An answer FACE cannot read (an error page, an unexpected or partial response) is shown as not checked, never as “no exclusions”.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: The check decides nothing. A person reviews the findings and decides whether to work with the business. FACE does not block, reject, blacklist or notify anyone.
data.model#Model:
The findings are read from coded registry fields and computed on the deployment. No model decides them.
The optional summary uses the general reasoning tier.
data.not-a-consumer-report#Not a consumer rep: This is business due diligence. It runs on businesses only and has no way to name a private individual. It is not a consumer report, and it must not be used to make or support decisions about any person’s credit, employment, housing or insurance. A name match on a sanctions list is not an identification: only a person can confirm or dismiss it.
data.thresholds#Thresholds: The checks consider how recently an operating authority or company was established and whether a load is high-value. Each cut-off can be changed for a deployment, or for your organisation by an admin under Admin → Public registries & market data.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It runs business due diligence on a carrier, broker, freight forwarder, shipper or consignee from public registries and sanctions lists, and from your own history with that business. It produces findings for a person to review, never a rating. Its jobs:
Operating authority. Whether the US motor carrier or broker authority is active, and whether a revocation is pending. Insurance on file. Liability insurance against the required minimum, and cargo insurance or a broker’s bond where one is required. Safety and orders. The published safety rating and any out-of-service order in force. Authority age. When the authority was first granted. A very new authority on a high-value load is a red flag. Sanctions screening. The business name and the registered names against the OFAC SDN list, the EU consolidated list and the UK Sanctions List. Company registries. Legal name, status and registration from GLEIF (by LEI), SEC EDGAR (by CIK) and UK Companies House (by company number): an inactive or lapsed entity, a company in liquidation or dissolved, an insolvency history, a recently incorporated company, and a registered name that differs from the one given. Exclusions. Active SAM.gov exclusions (debarment or suspension), by Unique Entity ID. Your own history. Loads, on-time share, claims and disputes with this business in your records.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Findings, each with its source, a link to check it, and when it was retrieved. Red flags among them: revoked or inactive authority, insurance below the required minimum, an unsatisfactory safety rating, an out-of-service order, a very new authority on a high-value load, and any sanctions name match. Sanctions matches, always shown as a possible match that needs human review. Every source considered, including the ones not checked and why. At most one recommended action: a review by the Compliance Manager. The thresholds it applied.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: US FMCSA public carrier data (company census, licensing and insurance, authority history, out-of-service orders), by the USDOT or MC number you give. OFAC SDN list (U.S. Treasury), the EU consolidated financial sanctions list (European Commission) and the UK Sanctions List (FCDO), downloaded in full and screened on the deployment. GLEIF Legal Entity Identifier records (CC0), SEC EDGAR company submissions (U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission), UK Companies House company profiles (Open Government Licence) and SAM.gov exclusions (U.S. General Services Administration), each by the identifier you give. Your own lane history and account records. These registries were chosen because each is public, free, usable commercially, has an API keyed by an identifier, and registers companies. Where a registry can also hold a person (an LEI registered to a sole proprietor, an individual EDGAR filer), the record is reported only as such, with no name. Court dockets are not consulted. A source that is not given an identifier, or whose API key is not configured on your deployment, is listed as not checked with that reason.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan. Registries are contacted for every organisation, unless the deployment has turned live public data off. The only values sent are the identifiers you typed: USDOT, MC, LEI, CIK, UK company number or SAM.gov UEI. Sanctions lists are downloaded whole and screened locally, so the business name never leaves the deployment. SAM.gov and Companies House need a free API key, configured per deployment as a secret; the key is never shown, logged or passed to a model. Everything fetched is cached with its retrieval time. See Facts shared by every card.

data: Agent: the customer analysis (customer_analysis), run from the Customers tab of the Market & due diligence page (/market_diligence?tab=…). No page in the FACE app links to it today; it opens from its address.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Business accounts only. Rows that describe an individual or a consumer are excluded and counted, never analysed. Refuses to profile or track an individual person. Refuses to price or segment by protected characteristics. Refuses to inflate, hide or adjust cost to serve, margin, OTIF or payment figures. Recommends only. It does not send notices or terminate contracts.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: Cost to serve is what your rows state. Overheads your records do not allocate to orders are not in it, and a missing cost is never treated as zero. A churn signal is a pattern in your records, not a prediction that an account will leave. Days to pay is measured over paid invoices only. Concentration is computed in the currency with the most revenue; accounts in other currencies are not added to it.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: Every recommended action is a draft. Sending one for approval puts it in the approval queue, where a named person approves or rejects it. FACE does not change a price, send a notice or close an account.
data.model#Model:
The figures and the recommended actions are fixed arithmetic over your records. No model computes them.
The optional summary uses the general reasoning tier.
data.thresholds#Thresholds:
Each has a default and can be changed for a deployment, or for your organisation by an admin under Admin → Public registries & market data. Every result shows the thresholds it applied.
Threshold Default OTIF below which a service-level review is suggested 90% Days to pay above which a payment-terms review is suggested 60 One account’s share of revenue above which concentration is flagged 25%
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It analyses your shipper and consignee business accounts from your own records and suggests re-pricing, service-level and account reviews for a person to decide. Its jobs:
Cost to serve and margin. Activity-based cost to serve per account: transport, warehousing, handling, order processing, returns and other costs, as your records state them, with the margin on the orders that state both revenue and a cost. Service. OTIF (on time and in full) per account. Claims and disputes. Claim and dispute rates per account. Payment behaviour. Days from invoice to payment, weighted by amount, and open receivables. Concentration. Each account’s share of revenue, the top-three share and the Herfindahl-Hirschman index. Churn signals. Order volume falling, no recent orders, service levels falling and disputes rising, each with the figures behind it.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Per-account figures, with the number of rows behind each. Concentration figures and flags. Recommended actions, each naming who decides: re-pricing (Commercial Pricing Manager), service-level and account reviews (Account Manager), payment terms (Credit Controller), concentration (Commercial Director). On request, a short written summary. It phrases the figures above and adds none.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Your own account records: one row per order, with the account, its type, dates, revenue, activity costs, delivery outcome, claims, disputes and invoice and payment dates. A connection is marked as account records by the operator. No public data is used.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan, and nothing leaves the deployment. See Facts shared by every card.

data: Agent: the documentation agent (documentation in ExecuteLoop), with the customs cards and the CUSTOMS_MANIFEST_EXCEPTION evidence document.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Refuses to falsify or fabricate HS codes, commercial invoices, packing lists or Incoterms to avoid a tariff or a check. Never invents a figure. A document or value that isn’t on file is named as missing. Duty is kept out of avoidable port charges, so a delay’s cost isn’t inflated.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: It gives no legal or customs advice. A computed date or limit is an input for the person deciding. A draft document is only as complete as the ERP record behind it. Missing fields stay empty and are named, never filled with a plausible value. It doesn’t establish who caused a hold. It reports what the entry record says.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: The customs or trade lead approves every next step and every document before it is sent or filed. The agent never files a declaration, submits a document to an authority or amends a manifest on its own. HS classifications are proposals. The declarant remains responsible for them.
data.model#Model:
The deployment’s general reasoning tier.
The customs exception document is fixed arithmetic over cited records. No model computes its figures.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It reads your shipping and customs records, finds what is holding a shipment up or doesn’t match, and drafts the next document or step for your trade team. Its jobs:
Customs holds. Finds entries that are held, which release documents are still missing, and the charges that have built up so far. Document cross-checks. Compares the bill of lading, commercial invoice and packing list for one shipment, and names where they disagree. Weight against manifest. When the weighbridge and the manifest differ by more than 5 %, drafts a manifest amendment. Draft trade documents. When an order is ready for dispatch, drafts the bill of lading, commercial invoice, packing list and customs declaration from your ERP records, with the HS classification and Incoterm for review.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Customs cards with a priority and a proposed next action, such as “request the certificate of origin from the supplier”. A customs manifest exception waits on Actionable Twins under the disruptions play. The CUSTOMS_MANIFEST_EXCEPTION evidence document, with each figure cited. See Evidence documents. Draft document payloads (bill of lading, commercial invoice, packing list, customs declaration), an HS classification and the Incoterm, for a person to check.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Customs entry records, manifests, bills of lading, commercial invoices, packing lists, weighbridge events, ERP order and shipping records, regulatory tables you provide, and the rules Rules Recon found in your data. It can run read-only queries against the connection a run was started with.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan. See Facts shared by every card.

data: Agent: the posture agent (ai_posture), behind PostureService.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Builds the domain map from your schemas and samples. It doesn’t invent tables or domains. Refuses to inflate readiness scores or data-quality grades without evidence. Refuses to suggest or test dangerously open security settings, or to alter audit logs. Doesn’t penalise vendors or regions on assumptions rather than measured evidence. Stays on posture: fulfilment and claims belong to other agents.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: A grade reflects the structure of the data it could read, not how the data is used. A failed scan is an error, not a grade of F. A domain that couldn’t be read is not assessed, which is different from a pass. Business-meaning links between domains are the model’s inference. Check them before relying on them.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: The data owner decides on every recommendation. The agent never changes schemas, masking or access.
data.model#Model:
The deployment’s general reasoning tier.
FACE’s health score and letter grade also have a deterministic path that uses no model; Posture & maturity says which result came from where.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It reads your connected tables and documents, groups them into business domains, and grades how ready each domain is to be relied on, with the issues behind each grade. Its jobs:
Map the estate. Groups tables that share keys, entities or subject into domains, and names how each domain relates to the others, including links of business meaning where no key is shared. Grade each domain. Gives an A–F grade with six readiness measures (quality, risk, lineage, freshness, policy and cost) and the concrete issues driving the grade. Name the incidents. Writes up material data-maturity incidents with severity, impact, root cause, blast radius and a recommended fix.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A posture snapshot: domains, their relationships, a maturity scorecard and incidents, shown on Why. Results the agent wrote are marked as model-generated. See Posture & maturity.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Table schemas, sample rows and extracted documents from the connections you configure. Exploring a source never samples customer rows; reading rows is a separate, bounded call (see Data sources).
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan. See Facts shared by every card.

data:
What it is: FACE’s image work: grading camera frames (Vision & CCTV), the vision agent (vision), reading photographed or scanned forms, and proposing elements from a picture of a site plan.
Runs on the Server’s vision model, which starts on demand. The first image request after a quiet period takes longer while the model loads.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: A person is not a subject. People never appear in the graded objects, and a frame with no inspectable object gets no grade rather than a low one. A detector’s class is never written into a graded label. Refuses to downgrade, hide or fake a camera assessment. Refuses to steer a sensor cue into unlocking a crane, blinding a camera or standing down a safety interlock, and refuses to plant false events into the shared operational picture. A model’s confidence in a value it read from a document is recorded, never used as a truth threshold.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: A grade and a damage percentage are the vision model’s estimate from downscaled pixels. They aren’t a physical inspection. A retained evidence frame shows the reviewer what was assessed. It isn’t a forensic record. It identifies no one.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: Nothing a vision model proposes from a plan is written to the twin graph until an operator confirms it. See Twin ontology & graph. A grade is input for a person. It never approves, rejects or releases anything. Any action taken on what a frame or a form shows goes through the same action-card approval as everything else.
data.model#Model:
The deployment’s vision tier, started on demand.
The live camera view uses a local detector only and never calls the vision model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It reads images and turns them into fields, grades and proposed elements that FACE and a person can check. Its jobs:
Camera frames. Grades the inspectable object in a frame: what it is, its material, a damage grade (PRISTINE, DAMAGED, DEFECTIVE or DESTROYED) and an estimated damage percentage. Optional detection draws one box per object of the graded class. Forms. Reads a photographed or scanned document, such as a bill of lading, packing list or delivery note, when text extraction alone can’t. Site plans. Proposes zones, docks and yard slots from a picture of a plan, for an operator to confirm.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A graded frame with per-object results, each box labelled with the stage that drew it, and notes that explain any absence. See Vision & CCTV. Values read from a document image, each recorded with the outcome of the read (READ, NOT_PRESENT_ON_DOCUMENT, ILLEGIBLE or EXTRACTION_FAILED). You attach a document with the clip or camera on Ask, and Why shows what was attached to the run. See Evidence documents. Proposed plan elements, which stay proposals until an operator confirms them, in the Site plans panel on Actionable Twins › Map. See Twin ontology & graph.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Frames pushed to FACE or sampled from RTSP/HTTP camera feeds, document images, and plan images. Frames are downscaled before the model sees them.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane. No outside AI service is called on any plan. Images travel in their own typed field, never as text inside a prompt. See Sovereign models.

data: What it is: the field-reading narrative, which writes up a walk with a handheld reader such as the Flipper edge reader.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Never computes, rounds, corrects or reconciles a figure. If two figures look inconsistent, it names both and leaves them unresolved. Never writes a reading with no value as a measurement. Never presents an ambient reading as support for the walk’s claim. An enclosure or device temperature measures the equipment, never the cargo, and the paragraph keeps that qualifier.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: A sighting says a thing was heard. It isn’t a location, a count or an inventory. Radio occupancy says a band was busy, not what was transmitting. It doesn’t identify people or say whether anyone was authorised to be there.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: The paragraph is a report. It proposes no action. Any action on a site walk is a person’s decision. It changes no figure. Every number in it is given to it and frozen.
data.model#Model:
The deployment’s general reasoning tier.
The narrative records which model wrote it. The readings and their classification are set before the model is called.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It turns what a handheld reader picked up on a site walk into one plain paragraph that says what was found and, just as clearly, what the walk does not establish. Its jobs:
Phrase the walk. Writes one paragraph over readings that have already been decided, without changing any of them. Keep the distinctions. Keeps apart: a reading with no value and a reading of zero; “absent” (the sensor was driven and nothing answered) and “unstable” (something is there, but it isn’t a measurement); readings that support the walk’s claim and ambient readings taken at the same time; a gap (nobody was standing there) and an outage, which a gap never is. Say what it doesn’t prove. Includes the walk’s “what this does not establish” sentence every time.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: One short paragraph, with no headings, bullets, recommendations or next steps. When the paragraph can’t be written from the input alone, it says exactly what is missing instead.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The frozen readings of one walk as the reader’s connector reported them, such as NFC, 125 kHz RFID, infrared, sub-GHz, 1-Wire and Wi-Fi sightings, with each reading’s role and quality, and the walk’s own statement of what it doesn’t establish.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan. Labels from a field reader are treated as untrusted, because anyone nearby can influence what a radio reader hears. See Facts shared by every card.

data: Agent: the fraud indicator agent (fraud_detection in ExecuteLoop), with the FRAUD_INDICATOR_REVIEW evidence document and the ReviewFraudIndicators call.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: No profiling: it never uses or infers gender, race, ethnicity, religion, nationality, age, disability, a name, an address or a neighbourhood. Never looks into anyone’s private life, social media, family, criminal record or credit. Refuses to label anyone a fraudster or as guilty, and refuses to hold or deny a payment without a person. Refuses to hide or drop an indicator for a particular party. Each drafted check is screened against these rules as output, before it reaches you.
data.how-the-likelihood-band-is-set#How the l: The band comes from fixed rules and statistics over your cited records. No model sets or moves a band. Every card states the review settings in force and where they came from.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: This is not a consumer report. It must not be used for decisions about an individual’s credit, employment or insurance. It works from your records. A pattern can have an innocent explanation the records do not show, which is why every indicator ends in a check, not a conclusion.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A named claims or special-investigations reviewer decides each indicator, with one of two choices. Dismiss needs a reason, which is recorded. Escalate opens an investigation case for that reviewer. Both are written to the decision log. An indicator is never “approved”. The agent never accuses anyone, never holds, blocks or denies a payment, claim or refund, and never contacts the party named. An indicator is not for sending to the party it names.
data.model#Model:
The deployment’s general reasoning tier.
The indicators, bands and amounts are fixed rules and statistics over cited records. The agent orders the indicators and phrases the next check; the server takes bands and amounts from the card, and every drafted step is checked before you see it.
data.review-settings#Review settings: The review settings can be adjusted for your deployment. Set FACE_INDICATOR_THRESHOLDS_FILE to a JSON file that names only the values you change. A file that cannot be read or is out of range is not applied, and every card says the override was invalid.
data.what-it-does#What it does: It flags records in your own logistics and claims data that a claims or special-investigations reviewer should check, and drafts the check. It never accuses anyone. It looks across invoices, payments, claims, deliveries, carrier records, payee details and returns for irregularities that warrant a check.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A FRAUD_INDICATOR_REVIEW evidence document per indicator on Actionable Twins (claims play): the evidence behind it, each item citing its records, a likelihood band (low, medium or high), the amount on the flagged records where one is stated, and one next check. From ReviewFraudIndicators: the indicators at or above a band you choose, and, if you ask, a drafted check per indicator. Each check is a concrete verification step and names its reviewer.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Payments, claims, carrier invoices with their rate confirmations, receiving (OS&D) records, tracking telemetry and returns records. Everything is keyed by a business record: an invoice, a payment, a claim, a load, a carrier, a payee or a returns account.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan. Your records reach the model as fenced, untrusted data. See Facts shared by every card.

data: Agent: the finance agent (finance in ExecuteLoop), with the rate-confirmation and SLA evidence documents.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Compares your invoice with your own rate confirmation, line by line. A rate the confirmation doesn’t state is reported as not stated, not disputed on a guess. Refuses to falsify cost-benefit, total-cost-of-ownership or cost-to-serve results. Refuses to fabricate or hide procurement spend to favour a vendor, and refuses to invent market-rate benchmarks. Stays on finance: claims disputes, dispatch, maintenance schedules and compliance audits belong to other agents.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: Its reference is your contract: every figure is measured against your own rate confirmation. Identified money is not recovered money. Only what a carrier credits or pays back is recovered. A transaction category comes with the agent’s confidence. It is a suggestion for your chart of accounts, not a posting. When the contract, the invoice line or the SLA clause is missing, the figure is reported as missing and no amount is given.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: An accounts-payable or finance lead approves every short-pay, dispute and credit request. The agent never pays, withholds or credits money itself. Budget reallocations and procurement changes it suggests are recommendations only.
data.model#Model:
The deployment’s general reasoning tier.
The audit documents’ amounts are fixed arithmetic over your invoice and rate confirmation. No model computes them.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It checks what carriers bill against what you agreed, and drafts the short-pay or credit request for finance to approve. Its jobs:
Invoice against rate confirmation. Finds accessorial lines that the rate confirmation doesn’t authorise, units billed inside free time, and rates above the one agreed. SLA credits. Works out the service credits owed under an SLA clause for late pickups or missed delivery windows. Order, invoice and bill of lading. Finds where the three disagree on quantity, and by how much. Spend oversight. Sorts transactions into categories with a stated confidence, flags spend that departs from its baseline, and compares options by cost-benefit, total cost of ownership and cost to serve.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Evidence documents RATE_CON_ACCESSORIAL_AUDIT (accessorials billed above the rate confirmation) and MSA_SLA_COMPLIANCE_AUDIT (service credits owed). Their headline amounts count as money only as described on Action cards & money. Action cards proposing a short-pay, a dispute or a credit request, on Actionable Twins under the claims play. For spend oversight: categorised transactions with a confidence, anomalies with the observed and expected values side by side, and recommended actions.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Carrier invoices, signed rate confirmations, master service agreements and their SLA clauses, purchase orders, goods-received records, invoice lines, the general-ledger chart you use, and the rules Rules Recon found in your data. It can run read-only queries against the connection a run was started with.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan. See Facts shared by every card.

data: Agent: the freight market analyst (freight_market), run from the Freight market tab of the Market & due diligence page (/market_diligence?tab=…). No page in the FACE app links to it today; it opens from its address.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: The comparison is your own history plus public fuel data. It uses no proprietary rate index and refuses to make up a market or spot rate. Refuses to steer a re-bid or consolidation towards a favoured carrier. Recommends only. It does not book, tender, award or pay. A written summary that states a figure the analysis did not compute, or proposes an action outside its allowed set, is not shown.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: A lane is measured against its own history. A lane above its own trend is not proof it is above the market. The BTS index covers all US freight. It is context, not a lane benchmark. A fuel surcharge moving faster than diesel is a reason to check your contract’s fuel table, not proof of an error. A row without a linehaul rate, a distance or a distance unit is not used, and is counted with the reason. Nothing is filled in. With no network or no permission to reach the public sources, the lane figures still work; the fuel comparison is marked not checked.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: Every recommended action is a draft. Sending one for approval puts it in the approval queue, where a named person approves or rejects it. Approving records the decision. FACE contacts no carrier, sends no tender and awards no freight.
data.model#Model:
The figures and the recommended actions are fixed arithmetic over your records and the public sources. No model computes them.
The optional summary uses the general reasoning tier.
data.thresholds#Thresholds:
Each threshold has a default and can be changed for a deployment, or for your organisation by an admin under Admin → Public registries & market data. Every result shows the thresholds it applied.
Threshold Default Lane above its own baseline by more than 10% Tender rejection share that flags a lane 20% Fewest tenders before the rejection share counts 5
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It benchmarks each of your lanes against that lane’s own history, and suggests re-bid, consolidation and fuel-surcharge reviews for your procurement team to decide. Its jobs:
Rate trend. The median linehaul rate per mile or kilometre over the last 90 days of a lane’s records, against the 275 days before. A lane above its own baseline by more than the threshold (10% by default), with enough loads in both windows, is flagged. Seasonal comparison. The same 90 days a year earlier, so a seasonal peak is not mistaken for a trend. Tender rejections. How many of your tenders on the lane were rejected. Fuel surcharge against diesel. How your fuel surcharge per distance moved against the US EIA weekly diesel price over the same weeks. Transit and accessorials. Mean transit days, on-time share against planned transit, and accessorial charges per load. Candidates. Re-bid candidates (above own trend, or many rejections), consolidation candidates (thin lanes from one origin to one destination region), and fuel-surcharge reviews.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Lane benchmarks with every figure, the windows they cover and the number of loads behind them. Flags with the figures that raised them. Recommended actions, each naming the Transportation Procurement Manager as the person who decides. The list of sources consulted, each marked live, cached, stale or not checked, with its retrieval time, and the rows of your records that could not be used and why. On request, a short written summary. It phrases the figures above and adds none.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads:
Your own lane history: the loads and tenders your systems record, with origin, destination, dates, tender outcome, linehaul, fuel surcharge, accessorials, distance and its unit, and transit days. A connection is marked as lane history by the operator.
Two public sources, as context:
US EIA weekly retail on-highway diesel price (U.S. Energy Information Administration, public domain). BTS Freight Transportation Services Index (U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics, public domain), shown as national context only.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan. The two public sources are fetched for every organisation, unless the deployment has turned live public data off. They are cached with their retrieval time; nothing from your records is sent to them. See Facts shared by every card.

data: What it is: FACE’s cargo insurance evidence documents, and the general model when you ask questions about a file.
data.guardrails#Guardrails:
The documents are built to these policies:
Never invents a warranty condition the policy doesn’t state, for example a temperature band inferred from the word “reefer”. Never reads a missing declared value as zero, and never substitutes an invoiced value for an undeclared one. Never states that something caused a loss unless the records say so. A temperature reading and a crushed carton are two facts, not a cause and an effect. Never leaves out a loss figure the records state, and never discourages a claim. Never treats protected characteristics, or postcode and nationality as proxies for them, as grounds for anything.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: A document is a file, not a decision. It doesn’t establish that a loss is or isn’t covered. It works from the records you hold. FACE’s approval tiers govern who may approve an action inside FACE; a claim handler’s delegated authority stays with your own process (see Auditability & lineage). A free-text answer from the general model is the model’s reading of the file, not a document. Check it against the cited records.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: The adjuster, or another person with authority, decides. The agent never underwrites, prices a risk, accepts or declines cover, sets a reserve or settles a claim. No finding code says VOID, DECLINED, REPUDIATED or anything like it. Those are an underwriter’s words. Approving a card seals its document and records who approved it.
data.model#Model:
The documents on this card are built by fixed arithmetic over cited records. No model is involved in them. A model may phrase a document’s narrative only after its figures are set.
Questions you ask about a file in free text go to the general reasoning tier.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It assembles the cargo claim file for an adjuster, so the adjuster starts from the records rather than from a search. It never decides cover. Its jobs:
First notice of loss. Builds the FNOL document from the loss records, and names what hasn’t been stated. Cargo loss survey. Sets out what was lost or damaged, and its value, from the records. Warranty compliance audit. Checks the shipment’s records against the warranty conditions the policy states, such as a temperature band. Recovery. Prepares the subrogation demand against the carrier.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Evidence documents FNOL, CARGO_LOSS_SURVEY, WARRANTY_COMPLIANCE_AUDIT and SUBROGATION_DEMAND, each attached to an action card with one proposed next step. The cards wait on Actionable Twins; the FNOL, survey and subrogation cards sit under the claims play. Every fact cites the record it came from, and a missing figure is recorded as absent with a reason. See Evidence documents.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The policy records you hold (wording, warranties, declared value, deductible), certificates, loss reports, temperature and custody records, carrier contracts and the claim’s own documents.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan. See Facts shared by every card.

data: Agent: the predictive maintenance agent (predictive_maintenance in ExecuteLoop), with the EQUIPMENT_LIMIT_APPROACH evidence document and the AnalyzeTelemetry API call. Its cards wait on Actionable Twins under the maintenance play.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Uses only the limit your feed or the maker states. It never substitutes an industry norm or another asset’s limit. Refuses to override safety shutdowns, alarms or hazardous-materials procedures. Refuses to alter or delete maintenance and compliance records, or sensor and telematics data. Doesn’t neglect the safety needs of particular sites or regions when it ranks work.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: A trend is not a forecast. It gives no failure probability, confidence score or remaining useful life. A straight line through two readings supports none of them. With no stated limit, or too few readings, it writes no limit card and says why. When readings wander instead of trending, it says the crossing can’t be projected.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A maintenance planner or supervisor approves every repair, shutdown, parts order and schedule change. The agent never shuts equipment down, overrides an alarm or orders parts itself.
data.model#Model:
The deployment’s general reasoning tier.
The limit-approach document is fixed arithmetic over cited readings. Nothing is fitted and nothing is forecast.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It reads equipment sensor logs, says how far each asset is from the limit its feed states and in which order to act, and drafts the intervention for a maintenance planner. Its jobs:
Trend to a stated limit. Reports the margin left and, when the readings move steadily towards the limit, when a straight line through the first and last readings would reach it. Prioritise. Orders the work by safety first, then by the impact on dependent lines and shipments. Plan the work. Drafts the work order, a maintenance window in the nearest planned downtime, and a spare-parts request when stock is below the reorder point your inventory feed states.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: The EQUIPMENT_LIMIT_APPROACH evidence document, with the readings it used, so a technician can redo the sum. See Evidence documents. Action cards with a priority and a proposed intervention. Draft work orders and parts requests.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Equipment readings such as vibration, bearing and oil temperature, pressure and battery state; the limits the feed or maker states; maintenance logs; production schedules; and spare-part stock levels. It can run read-only queries against the connection a run was started with.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan. See Facts shared by every card.

data: What it is: what you use on Simulate › Options to see what you could do about a run’s findings and what each option is worth, and FACE’s decision-authority policy, which decides who must approve each action on Actionable Twins.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Comparing options reads only what the run stored. It never re-reads a source. Every scenario figure is worked out from the assumptions you state. When a discount rate isn’t stated, the default is shown. Refuses scenarios that assume one demographic group is superior to another, or that attribute failures to protected groups. Refuses scenarios aimed at price fixing, predatory or discriminatory pricing, market cornering or sabotage. Refuses to skew forecasts to influence orders or budgets, or to hide anomalies. Stays on analysis: booking freight or writing rules belong elsewhere.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: An option’s figure covers the rows the run read. A fetch reads a bounded sample of each table, and the card says so when it did. Read whether an effect was estimated or assumed. A lead-time option’s effect is estimated from the shipments that took it. A temperature option assumes every reading moves by the full change, and the card says that effect is not estimated. “No clear winner” is an answer. It means the ranges overlap on this data, not that FACE failed. A scenario result is your own assumptions written out formally. It isn’t a prediction of what will happen. The scenarios in a run cover only what was simulated: read the counts before treating the results as covering the whole estate. The approval tier says who must approve. A recorded approval shows who approved, not how carefully they reviewed.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: Options executes nothing and changes nothing in your systems. Sending an option for approval is a separate act by a person, and approving it records the decision; it runs nothing by itself. An option sent for approval is never automatic. It needs one named person, or two different named people, as the policy answers it. When no approval rule matches, the default is one named approver, never automatic. Safety and regulatory actions always need a person, and a dual approval needs two different people. Every decision is written to the hash-chained decision log before anything runs. If it can’t be logged, nothing runs. See Auditability & lineage.
data.model#Model: Comparing options uses no model. The scores and ranges are arithmetic over the rows the run stored. Scenarios and their explanation: the general reasoning tier. The approval policy uses no model. It is fixed policy code. Causal and Bayesian analysis runs in the statistics engine, not in the language model. See Statistics & ML.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It lays out the choices before anyone commits money, and makes sure the decision to act is taken by the right number of named people. Its jobs:
Options. For the decision behind the selected run’s checks, it scores each option on one shared measure with a 95% range. It marks one Recommended only when that option’s range clears the next one’s and the figure as measured. Otherwise it says No clear winner on this data, and why. Scenarios. It generates scenarios from your estate’s domains, links and rules, and tests them against your data. Options lists them under “What FACE tested”, with a Graph view and a New Simulation action. Cost and benefit. When you state the costs and benefits of a change, the scenario agent is asked to work out net present value (at 8 % when no discount rate is given) and payback, and to flag payback above 36 months as high risk. Approval tier. For each proposed action, the policy names the tier: advisory, one named approver, two different named approvers, automatic, or denied.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Option cards on Options. Each shows the lever and the change, what it was measured to do over the run’s rows with its range, and whether it was recommended. An option the data cannot score is Not measured, with the data it needs, and is never ranked. Scenario results on Options: what each scenario tested and how it ended. The status counts, what went to the twins and the run step by step are in the folded How FACE knows this. See Simulate and Simulation & twins. A card on Actionable Twins when you press Send for approval. It lands in Waiting for you and shows the person approving it what they are approving. See Action cards & money. For each card, its approval tier and the rule that set it.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The selected run’s checks and the figures it measured, your estate’s domains and rules, the scenario parameters you set in New Simulation, time series and operational records, and the output of the statistics engine. The approval policy reads an action’s type, value and safety or regulatory flags.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan. See Facts shared by every card.

data: Agent: the reverse logistics agent (reverse_logistics in ExecuteLoop), with dock triage (TriageReturnItem) and the RETURN_DISPOSITION evidence document.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Follows your written disposition policy. The answer for a grade doesn’t depend on who is on the dock. A grade it doesn’t recognise is refused, never guessed. Uses your own grading and repair figures. It looks up no secondary-market prices. Doesn’t grade returns differently because of who the customer is. Refuses to inflate refurbishment grades or to record a disposal as recycling. Refuses to route hazardous or electronic waste improperly, or to skip e-waste certification.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: It doesn’t issue refunds or credits, or move stock. A pattern of returns that looks unusual is a lead for a person to check, not a finding of abuse. It doesn’t certify disposal of hazardous or electronic waste.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: The returns supervisor makes the disposition call and approves any response to the customer. Triage moves no stock and raises no credit or refund.
data.model#Model: Dock triage uses no model. It is fixed arithmetic: the same grade always gets the same answer. The agent’s reasoning uses the general reasoning tier.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It checks each return against the contract window and the authorisation, applies your disposition policy the same way every time, and drafts the call for the returns supervisor. Its jobs:
Window and quantities. Finds returns received after the contract window, units short of or over the authorisation, damaged units, and the value at stake. Disposition. Grades a returned item at the dock and proposes restock, refurbish, liquidate or recycle. Warranty and recovery. Checks warranty periods against the records you hold, and compares repair cost with expected recovery. Routing. Proposes where a return should go and which returns to collect together. Hand-off. Passes a claims question to the claims agent.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Dock triage results: the grade and the disposition it maps to. Recovery yield, refurbishment cost and a routing destination are not derived, because FACE holds no pricing, cost or facility data for returns, and every response says so. See Simulation & twins. The RETURN_DISPOSITION evidence document, with cited figures. Action cards with a proposed response to the customer or a routing step, on Actionable Twins under the fulfilment play.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Return authorisations, original delivery records, contract return windows, grading results and repair estimates, warranty records, and the capabilities of your returns facilities. It can run read-only queries against the connection a run was started with.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan. See Facts shared by every card.

data:
Agent: the self-healing agent, which watches FACE’s own health and the endpoints FACE depends on.
This agent acts on its own. It is the one FACE agent whose remediations run without a person approving each one, so that FACE recovers from a fault in seconds rather than waiting for someone to be paged. An operator can switch automatic remediation off with a deployment setting; it is on by default. See Configuration.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: A fixed list of permitted actions; anything else is refused. Unsure means notify, never act. No destructive or irreversible action, and no change to security controls. Requests and responses are screened by FACE’s guardrails like every other agent.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: It handles one event at a time. Causes that span several services are for a person to read from the notification and the log. A rollback reverts the most recent change that correlates with the fault, which is not always the cause.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: Automatic remediation is limited to the five actions above. It can never delete data, shut a host down or disable a security control (authentication, TLS or the circuit breaker itself). Every remediation is logged. Operators can turn automatic remediation off for the whole deployment, which narrows the agent to unhealthy-endpoint events. Everything else FACE recommends still waits for the named approver.
data.model#Model: Runs on the deployment’s general reasoning tier.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It receives one health event at a time and picks the single safest remediation from a fixed list:
Restart a runner or process that has stopped responding. Trip the circuit breaker to isolate a dependency that keeps failing. Roll back the most recent change that correlates with the fault. Scale to add capacity under sustained resource pressure. Notify a person when no safe automatic fix exists or the fault is ambiguous.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: One remediation from the list above, the target it applies to, a one-line rationale and a confidence between 0 and 1. A low-confidence or ambiguous case always becomes a notification for a person, not an action.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: A health event describing a degraded in-process resource (CPU, memory, goroutines, a panic) or an unreachable external endpoint.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: Inside your FACE deployment, on the deployment’s own inference. Health events stay in your deployment; no outside AI service is involved.

data: Agent: the fulfilment agent (fulfilment in ExecuteLoop), working with FACE’s statistics engine.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Uses the reorder points and bounds you set. It never invents them. Refuses to force an order through or bypass a budget. Doesn’t favour suppliers on demographics, and doesn’t starve particular regions or groups of stock during a shortage. Refuses to reorder dispatch to favour anyone over your SLA commitments. Refuses to ignore temperature excursions or suppress cold-chain alerts to save cost or time.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: A forecast is not “exact stock needs”. It comes with its method and the history it had, so you can judge how far to trust it. With too little history, the statistics engine declines to forecast rather than guessing.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A buyer approves every purchase order and expedite. The agent never places an order with a supplier on its own. Dispatch priorities and allocations it proposes are recommendations only.
data.model#Model:
The deployment’s general reasoning tier.
Forecasts come from FACE’s statistics engine, not from a language model. See Statistics & ML.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It reads stock, demand and lead times, says per item whether to do nothing, order now or expedite, and drafts the order for a buyer to approve. Its jobs:
Reorder decisions. Works out days of cover and states which of your reorder bounds was crossed, and by how much. Forecasts. Reads the statistics engine’s forecast, names the method that was used and how much history it had, and adjusts safety stock from it. Purchase orders. Drafts the order, with an expedite quantity and its premium freight cost kept separate from normal replenishment. Sourcing and service. Compares suppliers and carriers on the records you hold, measures on-time-in-full, and finds lanes worth consolidating. Dispatch documents. When an order is ready for dispatch, drafts the shipping documents (see Customs & trade documents).
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Action cards proposing a purchase order, an expedite or no action, each with the figures behind it, on Actionable Twins under the inventory play. Operational procedures, ranked by the money and time they save.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Stock on hand and on order, demand history, lead times, reorder points and bounds, supplier and carrier records, order and delivery records, and the rules Rules Recon found in your data. It can run read-only queries against the connection a run was started with.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan. See Facts shared by every card.

data: Agent: the voice dispatcher (voice), behind the phone line and the calling screen. The FACE app’s navigation has no calling page today: the calling screen is not one of its routes.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: The phone line is the one path a person can reach without an account, so every utterance is screened before any model is called. A refusal is spoken to the caller. See AI safety. Gives no arrival time unless a planning speed is stated. Distances are labelled as straight-line estimates.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: For a driver in distress it alerts a person. It gives no legal or medical advice. A transcript can mishear. Events it logs from speech are what the driver said, not vehicle telemetry.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A dispatcher acts on every alert and every routing change. A call never changes routes or stops in your transport system.
data.model#Model: Reasoning: the general reasoning tier. Speech recognition and speech synthesis run on services inside the deployment.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It lets a driver ask out loud where the next stop is, what the customer asked for or which door to use, and hear a short answer, with the call written to the log. Its jobs:
Answer the driver. Replies in a few spoken sentences from the dispatch record. Log what was said. Picks out the events a driver reports, such as speeding, a tyre-pressure warning, a long idle or an engine vibration, and writes them to the log. Alert a person. Raises anything urgent, such as a driver in distress, to a dispatcher.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A short spoken reply, synthesised as speech. Safety notifications and routing updates for a dispatcher. The telematics events the driver reported, for a dispatcher. The call itself is logged turn by turn.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The transcript of what the driver said, the vehicle’s position, the stop list and customer notes on the dispatch record, and the rules Rules Recon found in your data. Its only tool is a read-only query.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan. A phone call is carried by your telephony provider, which carries the audio. On a call, the audio is transcribed as it arrives and then discarded, and the transcript is kept with the session. A caller’s words are never written to the process log.

data: Agents: the twins orchestrator (twins), the route twin (route_twin) and the common operational picture (cop), with the yard, border, custody and disruption cards.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Never makes up a distance or a time. A route the provider couldn’t compute is “unavailable”, never zero. A missing cause, capacity or cost figure is reported as missing. Doesn’t deprioritise neighbourhoods or regions on socioeconomic or demographic grounds, and doesn’t recommend hoarding capacity or price gouging. Refuses to de-anonymise people from aggregate trends, and refuses to fabricate sustainability figures.
data.how-to-read-its-results#How to read its: An unrecorded handoff is not a break in custody. A ranked route is only as good as the provider’s answer and the criteria you named. An event flagged as single-source hasn’t been confirmed by a second source. It doesn’t establish who caused a delay beyond what the records state.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A supervisor approves every action on a card, through TwinsService.ExecuteAction. Rejection needs a reason. The agents never dispatch a vehicle, book a carrier or send anything to a transport system on their own. Every action an orchestrator’s final answer proposes passes the judging ladder before it reaches the queue. An action the judge still disagrees with after one revision is removed.
data.model#Model:
The deployment’s general reasoning tier.
Distances and travel times come from your routing provider, not from the model. The cards’ figures are fixed arithmetic over your records.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It reads yard snapshots, border and port events and transport records, flags the trailer, crossing or container that is costing money now, and drafts the action for the supervisor. Its jobs:
Yard capacity. Finds when the yard is over capacity and which arrivals were never recorded. Border waits. Works out detention from dwell time and the stated cost per hour, and proposes “transmit corrected documents” when the recorded cause is a document problem. Demurrage and detention. Separates days caused by documents from days caused by congestion. Service disruption. Records a disruption and its effect on open orders. Routes. Ranks the routes your routing provider returns on the criteria you name, with emissions per mode where a factor is stated. One picture. Ranks events from several sources by priority, life safety first, and flags events seen by only one source. Orchestration. The twins orchestrator maps each event to the right action card and hands work to the other agents on these cards.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Action cards on Actionable Twins, each with a priority and one proposed action. Route proposals also show on its Map view. See Action cards & money. Evidence documents such as CHAIN_OF_CUSTODY_AUDIT and SERVICE_DISRUPTION. A ranked list of routes and carriers, and a prioritised list of current events.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Yard snapshots and appointments, border crossing and port events, container free time and gate events, custody events, carrier and lane records, routes from your routing provider, sensor and camera findings, and the twin graph. It can run read-only queries against the connection a run was started with.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan. See Facts shared by every card.

data:
This section is for the platform and SRE teams who deploy, configure, upgrade and troubleshoot a FACE instance. It is also for Runink operators. FACE runs on the Runink platform: Runink TIDE’s operators on a k0s cluster. Each deployment runs one FACE instance, managed by TIDE, in the face-system namespace. FACE needs nothing outside that cluster to run. It calls no third-party model API and no managed cloud database, so the same procedures work air-gapped.
FACE is application code. TIDE provisions the cluster, runs the operators that build FACE’s pods, and serves the model plane FACE reasons with. The pages below say which side owns each setting, so you know whether to change a custom resource or the FACE image.
Deployment modelThe workloads in face-system, the ControlPlane resource, and what the operator injects. Prerequisites and orderingThe three secrets, the tenant and the inference URL that must exist before the image runs, and the exact boot refusals. Configuration referenceEvery environment variable the code reads, grouped, with defaults. Model planeThe OpenAI-compatible contract and bringing a plane up. Persistence and backupThe appfs root, object and record stores, what to back up, and custody of the key. RunnersOperating in-cluster fetch runners and self-hosted runners that enrol outbound. Upgrades and CDHow images are built and rolled, and what each upgrade leaves behind for a rollback. Health and troubleshootingProbes, boot refusals, crashloops, empty panels and sign-in failures.
data.the-rule-behind-most-incidents#The rule: FACE refuses to start when a dependency it cannot work without is missing. It does not fall back to a degraded mode. This applies to the session signing key, the mesh CA, the at-rest key and the inference endpoint. A crashlooping pod with one clear log line is the intended result of a configuration fault. A pod that runs but serves nothing would be harder to diagnose. So read the first ❌ line of the container log before you look anywhere else. Health and troubleshooting lists each one.

data:
This reference was built from the code. It lists every environment variable read by the FACE backend, the platform libraries it links, and the frontend. It leaves out variables read only by build tooling, benchmarks and tests, and variables read only by the separate voice calling-agent image.
In a cluster, set control-plane values through the ControlPlane resource’s env list, never on the live Deployment, and runner values in the face-runner manifest (see Deployment model). Locally, export them into the backend’s environment before you start it.
Secret in the Source column means the value is resolved through the platform secret backend (SECRET_BACKEND), so it can come from a mounted file instead of the environment. Everything else is read from the environment.
Connector and integration credentials (warehouses, SaaS APIs, maps keys) do not belong in environment variables. They are entered per connection in Settings › Integrations and stored sealed in FACE’s credential store. The few integration variables below are the exceptions the code still reads.
data.authentication#Authentication: Variable Source Default Purpose ADMIN_EMAIL env none The admin account created at boot. ADMIN_PASSWORD secret none Its password. If either value is missing, password admin login is disabled. AUTH_GOOGLE_ONLY env unset true makes Google sign-in the sign-in method; password sign-in shows Password sign-in is disabled — use Google sign-in. FACE_REQUIRE_TOTP env unset (off) Requires a TOTP second factor for password sign-in. all covers every account; a comma-separated list of roles (admin, writer, reader) covers only those roles. A covered account with no TOTP enrolled is not signed in by its password: the FACE app shows a setup key, and the first code from the authenticator app enrols the key and completes sign-in. Google sign-in relies on the identity provider’s own second factor. An unrecognised value stops the process. AUTH_SEED_USERS env none Comma-separated email=role pairs to seed. The operator projects them from ClientInstance users. AUTH_USERS_PATH env the data directory A legacy users file. It is imported once into the accounts table and then sealed as .migrated. OIDC_ISSUER env none The OIDC issuer. Single sign-on is on only when both this and OIDC_CLIENT_ID are set. OIDC_CLIENT_ID env none FACE’s OAuth client id, and the default token audience. It must equal the FACE app’s google_client_id (the face-frontend-config ConfigMap). OIDC_AUDIENCE env OIDC_CLIENT_ID An explicit audience override. OIDC_JWKS_URL env discovered An explicit JWKS URL instead of discovery. AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS env none The single sign-on allowlist. When SSO is configured and this is empty, every SSO login is refused (SSO is not available on this instance). An unlisted account gets This account is not authorized for this instance. The operator projects it from the face-oauth Secret. Changes take effect when the pod restarts. FACE_RECAPTCHA_SITE_KEY env none The reCAPTCHA v3 site (public) key for login. The FACE app reads it from GET /auth/config. Configure it with FACE_RECAPTCHA_SECRET_FILE to captcha-check logins. FACE_RECAPTCHA_SECRET_FILE secret path none Path to a file holding the reCAPTCHA secret key (a mounted Secret). It is read at each login, so a rotated Secret needs no restart. FACE_RECAPTCHA_HOSTNAMES env none Comma-separated FACE host(s) a token must have been minted on. Required once a key is present. With a key present but the configuration incomplete, every login is refused until it is complete. FACE_RECAPTCHA_MIN_SCORE env set by FACE Adjusts the reCAPTCHA v3 score a login must reach.
data.connectors-vision-and-integrations#Conne: Variable Default Purpose FACE_BROWSER_CONCURRENCY 12 The number of headless-Chrome renders run at once. Lower it on small hosts. FACE_MAP_TILE_URL unset An optional raster basemap for the twins map: an XYZ tile URL template ({z}, {x} and {y} all required) on your own tile service. Set, it is drawn instead of FACE’s built-in vector basemap. FACE never falls back to a public tile server. A template missing a placeholder is ignored, with a warning in the log. FACE_MAP_BASEMAP_PMTILES /app/basemap/basemap.pmtiles FACE’s built-in basemap: a PMTiles archive of OpenStreetMap vector tiles that ships in the server image and is served by the server itself at /api/map/basemap/{z}/{x}/{y}.mvt. Point it at a larger archive (for example a regional extract with street-level zooms) to give the map more detail. Missing, the map draws plain ground and says that no basemap is installed. FACE_MAP_GLYPHS_DIR /app/basemap/glyphs The glyphs the map draws place names with (/-.pbf), served at /api/map/glyphs/. Without them the map shows places as dots. FACE_MAP_TILE_ATTRIBUTION © OpenStreetMap contributors The credit shown on the map whenever the basemap is. Tiles built from OpenStreetMap data must carry it under the ODbL, self-hosted included; set your own if your tiles come from other data. FACE_MAX_DOWNLOAD_BYTES 2 GiB The largest file a connector downloads. SCRAPER_USER_AGENT Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; RuninkFACE/1.0) The user agent for crawling. VISION_DETECT_INSTANCES off true adds a per-instance detection turn per camera frame. It roughly doubles the vision time per frame. VISION_MAX_EDGE 448 Frames are downscaled to this longest edge. 0 disables downscaling. Keep it below 1000. VISION_SWEEP_FRAMES 2 The number of frames sampled per camera ingest (at most 8). VISION_RESOLVE_ITEMS off true resolves detected objects against the item catalogue. OCR_VISION_FALLBACK off true lets OCR fall back to the vision model. GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS_JSON secret A Google Workspace service-account JSON. The stored integration config is used when it is empty. TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID, TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN, TWILIO_FROM_NUMBER, TWILIO_WHATSAPP_FROM none Voice, SMS and WhatsApp. FACE refuses to send by name when they are missing. PUBLIC_URL localhost:8080 The public host used for Twilio media-stream callbacks. CALLING_AGENT_URL none The shared calling agent that WebRTC signalling is forwarded to. When it is unset, the call RPC answers Unavailable.
data.consensus-mesh-and-resilience#Consensus,: Variable Default Purpose RAFT_NODE_ID unset This node’s consensus id. When it is unset, the process does not join consensus (runners). When it is set, a failure to start the orchestrator stops the process. RAFT_PEERS none The peers, as id@host:port,…. RAFT_PIPE_DIR none The local proposal-pipe directory. RAFT_DATA_DIR unset (in memory) The durable consensus state. When it is unset, FACE warns that the state is memory-only. RAFT_MTLS_ADDR unset The listen address of the mTLS raft peer plane. A voting control plane must set it. RAFT_ADVERTISE_IP, RAFT_ADVERTISE_HOST none Extra IP and DNS SANs on the mesh leaf certificates. LOAD_SHED_THRESHOLD 0.85 The orchestrator’s load-shed threshold. SNAPSHOT_THRESHOLD, SNAPSHOT_RETAIN 1000, 100 Raft snapshot cadence and retention, in entries. WATCHDOG_CPU_THRESHOLD 99.5 The watchdog’s CPU alarm, in percent. WATCHDOG_MEMORY_THRESHOLD_MB library default The watchdog’s memory alarm. WATCHDOG_GOROUTINE_THRESHOLD 10000 The watchdog’s goroutine alarm. WATCHDOG_RUNNER_DIAL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 5 The runner reachability probe timeout. CIRCUIT_BREAKER_FAILURE_THRESHOLD 5 Failures before the breaker opens. CIRCUIT_BREAKER_RECOVERY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 30 How long the breaker stays open before it tries again. SELF_HEAL_AUTONOMOUS on false limits the self-healing reasoner to ENDPOINT_UNHEALTHY events.
data.embeddings#Embeddings: FACE does not embed. EMBEDDING_URL, MODEL_EMBEDDING_DIM, EMBEDDING_FORMAT and MODEL_EMBEDDING are not read, and setting them changes nothing. Retrieval is grep over plain text: see Grounding.
data.fetch-runners-and-agents#Fetch, runners: Variable Default Purpose MANAGED_RUNNER_ENDPOINT face-runner:7102 Where the control plane forwards fetches. REQUIRE_RUNNER_ISOLATION unset true makes an unreachable runner a hard failure instead of a fallback to the control plane’s in-process SQL service. RUNNER_PORT none The port used when dialling a configured runner endpoint that has none. RUNNER_ENROLL_ADDR unset On a self-hosted runner, the control-plane address it enrols with (see Runners). RUNNER_ENROLL_TOKEN none The service-account token the runner enrols with. It is required when the address is set. RUNNER_ENROLL_TLS true TLS with system roots for the enrolment dial. RUNNER_NAME, RUNNER_VERSION empty Shown in the control plane’s runner registry. RUNNER_COMPUTE_POOL, RUNNER_CPU_LIMIT, RUNNER_MEMORY_LIMIT none, 1, 1G Inputs to runink runner create for the Snowflake runner type. FACE_RUNNER_CHANNEL_ADDR, FACE_RUNNER_CHANNEL_LISTEN none The address runners in Snowflake or Databricks reach FACE’s runner channel at, and the local listen address. Both must be set for those deploy targets to be offered. FACE_RUNNER_CA_DIR none The runner CA (ca.crt, ca.key), read by path. FACE_RUNNER_IMAGE_ARCHIVE, FACE_RUNNER_IMAGE_ARCHIVE_SHA256, FACE_RUNNER_IMAGE_REF, FACE_RUNNER_BINARY, FACE_RUNNER_BINARY_SHA256 none The runner artifacts an on-premises deploy copies, each with its SHA-256. FACE_RUNNER_GCP_IMAGE none The default digest-pinned runner image in your registry for a Google Cloud deploy. SCHEDULE_EXECUTE_FETCH off true makes briefs run real fetches. When it is off, a brief’s trigger logs a dry run. The deployment sets it through spec.scheduleExecuteFetch. FETCH_CACHE_TTL 10m How long a fetch result may be reused. 0 disables reuse. FETCH_CACHE_MIN_CONFIDENCE 0.7 The minimum confidence for a cached result to be reused. FACE_RALPH_JUDGEMENT on Controls judging of proposed actions. FACE_RALPH_JUDGE_MAX_ACTIONS set by FACE Bounds the judging cost per answer. FACE_RALPH_JUDGE_REVISIONS set by FACE Bounds the revision rounds after dissent. FACE_FAST_JUDGEMENT on The local fast-path judge in front of the model. FACE_A2A_PEERS none Agent-to-agent delegation peers, separated by commas, spaces or newlines. A2A_ORGANIZATION falls back to RUNINK_ORG, then TIDE_GITHUB_ORG The organization published on the agent card. FACE_AGENT_EMAIL_ALLOWLIST none The addresses or @domain suffixes the audit trail treats as approved recipients for agent e-mail. Agent e-mail is always drafted for a person to send, whatever this list or the decision-authority policy says. FACE_OUTPUT_URL_HOSTS none Hosts an agent answer may link to, comma separated; a subdomain matches its parent. Every other link is removed from the answer, and images and embedded frames are always removed. FACE_GUARD_MODEL none The model-router token of the guard tier, usually guard. Configures the guard model that screens text in the agent loop. FACE_PROMPT_GUARD on Controls the guard model configured by FACE_GUARD_MODEL. The OpenBias rules and the output constraints always apply. FACE_AUTHORITY_POLICY_FILE embedded default A decision-authority policy (versioned JSON) replacing the shipped one. Unreadable or invalid = every approval refused.
