FACE_OPERATIONAL_LENS_FILE embedded default An operational lens (versioned JSON: areas, signals and the column-name terms that show them, and the decisions each needs) replacing the shipped one for the Operational coverage section on Ask. Unreadable or invalid = no lens, and the page says so. ENFORCE_AUDIT_LOGGING, REQUIRE_HITL, DATABASE_ENGINE, PRIMARY_SERVER_URL unset Reported into every compliance analysis as the controls in place.
data.frontend#Frontend: PORT (default 8080), WEB_DIR (/web) and BACKEND_ADDR. See Deployment model.
data.inference-and-the-model-plane#Inference:
Variable Default Purpose INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL none (required) The base URL for chat completions. INFERENCE_API_KEY empty Secret. Sent as Authorization: Bearer when it is set. FACE never generates one. The placeholder application-generated-key counts as empty. VISION_REMOTE_URL INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL The base URL for vision calls. VOICE_REMOTE_URL INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL The base URL for voice calls. INFERENCE_CONTEXT_SIZE 16384 The prompt window, in tokens, that the agent loop budgets against. INFERENCE_DECODE_TOK_S 3.4 The measured decode rate of the text tier. It sizes time budgets. INFERENCE_VISION_DECODE_TOK_S 1.0 The same, for the vision tier. REACT_DECODE_TOK_S INFERENCE_DECODE_TOK_S Overrides the decode rate for the agent loop’s turn budgets. POSTURE_DECODE_TOK_S INFERENCE_DECODE_TOK_S Overrides the decode rate for posture analysis. POSTURE_LLM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 120 The model time budget for posture analysis. COMPLIANCE_LLM_BUDGET_SECONDS 15 The model time budget for compliance analysis. METASEARCH_BUDGET_SECONDS 90 The time budget for the trend metasearch step of a fetch. FETCH_TREND_MAX_QUERIES 2 How many scenario market topics one fetch may search (1–6). Topics shared by the most scenarios go first; confirmed public names, when set, replace them. FACE_ADMIT_MAX 0 (off) The maximum number of concurrent inference calls. 0 dispatches directly with no scheduling. The operator sets 1. FACE_ADMIT_QUEUE 0 (unbounded) The maximum number of waiters before backpressure. The operator sets 32. FACE_ADMIT_MODE reject reject or degrade when the queue is full. FACE_ADMIT_WEIGHTS none Tier weights, for example interactive:4,batch:1. FACE_ADMIT_COALESCE off true lets identical concurrent prompts share one generation. FACE_GATE_MAX_INFLIGHT off The concurrent-submission cap of the inference gate. FACE_GATE_FIRST_TOKEN_SECONDS off The longest acceptable queue wait. The gate is on only when this or FACE_GATE_MAX_INFLIGHT is positive. FACE_GATE_DECODE_RATE none The measured tokens per second the gate assumes. FACE_GATE_REQUEST_SECONDS off The per-request time budget for inference calls. These variables are read into the process configuration for compatibility. FACE starts no model server of its own, so they neither choose nor tune what the plane serves. Set the model on the plane instead. They are: INFERENCE_PORT, INFERENCE_HOST, INFERENCE_MODEL, INFERENCE_TIMEOUT, INFERENCE_PARALLEL, INFERENCE_CACHE_RAM, INFERENCE_CPU_STRICT, INFERENCE_THREADS, INFERENCE_BATCH, INFERENCE_GPU_LAYERS, INTERNAL_INFERENCE_IP, INTERNAL_BRIDGE_IP, INTERNAL_SUBNET, MODEL_DIR, MODEL_VOXTRAL, MODEL_WHISPER and MODEL_VISION. (MODEL_VISION is also printed in the boot line that names the vision tier.)
MODEL_INFERENCE_TTS and MODEL_WAV_TOKENIZER were listed here and no longer exist. They were read into two config fields nothing in FACE ever consumed, and their names advertised a speech stack FACE does not have: it speaks through ui/voice’s VoiceService on the shared ttsd voice, and that is the only path that makes sound. Setting them never did anything; they are now gone rather than documented.
MODEL_VISION is a routing key, not a choice of weights. The model router selects a backend tier from this name and then rewrites the field to default before dispatch, so the value never reaches an engine — it only decides which engine. Use a logical tier token (vision); a weights filename classifies as the general TEXT tier, which answers an image request at HTTP 200 without seeing the image.
data.process-role-and-platform#Process, role: Variable Default Purpose SERVICE_ROLE control plane runner makes this process a fetch runner. Any other value makes it a control plane. The operator sets server or runner. PORT none The default for serve --port. The image entrypoint uses 7000 when PORT is unset. The operator sets 7100 (control plane) or 7102 (runner). APP_VERSION empty The version stamped on structured logs. SECRET_BACKEND env env or file. With file, secrets are read from SECRETS_DIR with the environment as fallback. Any other value makes every secret lookup fail. SECRETS_DIR /var/run/secrets The directory for the file backend. A file is named after the variable, or in lower case with dashes. RUNINK_VARIANT standard The declared variant, reported to the FACE app. It changes no data and no behaviour on any variant: FACE creates no connections and serves no rows of its own. FACE_LOCAL_INSTANCE false true offers a single local-development instance in the instance picker, on a process with no in-cluster ServiceAccount token only. In a cluster it changes nothing. RUNINK_APP face The app name that filters ClientInstances in the instance picker. FACE_CLIENT_INSTANCE none The name of this deployment’s own ClientInstance, used by the access page. There is no fallback. FACE_CLIENT_INSTANCE_NAMESPACE POD_NAMESPACE The namespace of that ClientInstance. POD_NAMESPACE none The pod’s namespace, from the downward API. Also used when publishing connectors to Runink TIDE. POD_NAME none The instance name on lineage reports sent to TIDE. HOSTNAME set by Kubernetes The runner id fallback when RUNNER_ID is unset. KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST, KUBERNETES_SERVICE_PORT kubernetes.default.svc, 443 The API server FACE lists ClientInstances from. FACE_CONNECTORS_APP face The app key of the connectors ConfigMap FACE publishes to TIDE, -connectors. Runink TIDE sets it on each instance to the exact key it created and granted. Unset (the control plane), FACE writes face-connectors. A value that is not a DNS-1123 label (at most 63 characters of a-z, 0-9 and -, starting and ending with a letter or digit) is logged and nothing is published. SUBSCRIPTION_TIER, SUBSCRIPTION_STATUS, SUBSCRIPTION_SEATS none The subscription the operator mirrors from the ClientInstance. A subscription is reported only when the tier is set and FACE_TENANT matches the tenant asked about. RUNINK_ACCOUNTS_FILE none The account file the platform operator provides, mapping each user to the purchaser whose billing account pays for their model time. Unset, every model call is recorded as unattributed and logged, never billed to another account. See Plans and billing. TIDE_ROUTER_BILLING_KEY_FILE, TIDE_ROUTER_BILLING_KID none The key file (read by path) and key id FACE signs each model call’s billing claim with. Unset, model calls carry no billing claim. It never blocks or fails a call. TIDE_ROUTER_IDENTITY_KEY none The model router’s key (base64, at least 32 bytes) FACE signs an identity assertion with for a fetch a person started, so it runs on the router’s interactive lane. It is never logged or sent to a client. Unset, every model call stays on its billing lane. TIDE_PLATFORM_ADMIN none The installation admin’s e-mail. That account sees every instance. When it is unset, nobody gets that grant. LICENSE none A signed licence blob, as base64 or raw JSON. LICENSE_FILE none A path to read the licence from when LICENSE is unset. LICENSE_PUBLIC_KEY none The base64 Ed25519 public key licences are verified against. FACE_MODEL_CAP_FETCH_PER_HOUR, FACE_MODEL_CAP_ASK_PER_HOUR, FACE_MODEL_CAP_LOOP_PER_HOUR, FACE_MODEL_CAP_SIMULATE_PER_HOUR, FACE_MODEL_CAP_VISION_PER_HOUR set by FACE How many model-backed runs one user may start per hour, per class: fetches (RunFetch, RunFetchStream), QuickAsk, agent loops (ExecuteLoop), simulations (SimulateScenario, InteractiveSimulate) and vision (ExtractText, IngestSurveillanceFeed). A call over the cap gets RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED with the time until the next slot. TIDE_HEALTH_URL, TIDE_HEALTH_TOKEN none Where FACE reports observed lineage to the TIDE console, and the bearer token it uses. CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS unset A comma-separated allowlist of browser origins for gRPC-web. Set it to the origin(s) the FACE app is served from. FACE_RATE_RPS, FACE_RATE_BURST set by FACE Configure the per-user request rate limit (sustained rate and burst). Callers over the limit get RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED. A value that does not parse keeps the default. ENV, GCP_REGION empty Labels printed into the system state that compliance and domain analyses read.
data.removed-and-renamed-names#Removed and re:
Since the TIDE rename (2026-10-19) FACE reads only the TIDE_* names above (TIDE_PLATFORM_ADMIN, TIDE_ROUTER_IDENTITY_KEY, TIDE_ROUTER_BILLING_KEY_FILE, TIDE_ROUTER_BILLING_KID, TIDE_HEALTH_URL, TIDE_HEALTH_TOKEN, TIDE_GITHUB_ORG, TIDE_ENVELOPE_KEK). The platform renders them; there is no fallback to the pre-TIDE spelling.
These are listed to help an upgrade. FACE ignores every one of them, except OBJECTSTORE_USE_SSL, which it refuses. Remove them from your resources.
Name Status REMOTE_LLAMA_URL, LLAMA_REMOTE_URL Renamed to INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL. A manifest that sets only the old name has no inference endpoint, and the process refuses to start. LLAMA_API_KEY Renamed to INFERENCE_API_KEY. MESH_MTLS, ENABLE_ALTS Removed. Mesh mTLS is unconditional. REQUIRE_MTLS_INGRESS Removed. OBJECTSTORE_USE_SSL Removed, and refused if it is set. Put the scheme in OBJECTSTORE_ENDPOINT. GOOGLE_API_KEY Read by no code. Maps keys are entered per connection in Settings › Integrations.
data.required-at-boot#Required at boot: Variable Source Purpose AUTH_JWT_SECRET secret Signs the pre-TOTP MFA challenge. The process refuses to start without it. MESH_CA_CERT secret The shared cluster CA certificate. Each pod issues its own rotating mTLS leaves from it. MESH_CA_KEY secret The shared cluster CA private key. TIDE_ENVELOPE_KEK secret A base64-encoded 32-byte key-encryption key for everything sealed at rest. INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL env The base URL of the shared inference plane. No other name is read for it. Prerequisites and ordering has the exact refusal messages.
data.storage-and-persistence#Storage and pers: Variable Source Default Purpose OBJECTSTORE_ENDPOINT env unset The object store (host:port or https://host:port). When it is unset, the appfs root uses an encrypted local directory. An endpoint without TLS is accepted only for a loopback or cluster-internal name. OBJECTSTORE_ACCESS_KEY, OBJECTSTORE_SECRET_KEY secret none Object-store credentials. They are required when an endpoint is set. OBJECTSTORE_VACUUM_ACCESS_KEY, OBJECTSTORE_VACUUM_SECRET_KEY secret none An optional second credential used for every delete. Set both or neither. OBJECTSTORE_BUCKET env core The object-store bucket for records, knowledge and evidence. The appfs root and the documents mount use their own buckets (FACE_APPFS_BUCKET, FACE_DOCUMENTS_BUCKET). FACE_APPFS_BUCKET env face The object-store bucket of the appfs root. Runink TIDE sets one per instance. It must be 3 to 63 characters of a-z, 0-9 and -, starting and ending with a letter or digit; any other value stops FACE from starting. FACE_DOCUMENTS_BUCKET env face-documents The object-store bucket of the documents mount, with the same rule. TIDE_ENVELOPE_KEK_RETIRED secret none Retired KEKs (comma- or space-separated, base64), accepted for decryption only. SQLITE_PATH /face.db A legacy face.db from an earlier build, imported once if it exists and never created. It also anchors the defaults below that say “beside face.db”. The entrypoint requires an absolute path. The operator does not set it. FACE_APPFS_DIR appfs/ beside face.db The encrypted local appfs root, used only when there is no object store. FACE_UPLOAD_DIR uploads/ beside face.db The instance’s private upload directory, created mode 0700. An OCR LOCAL source and a fetch attachment named by file name are read only from here, and uploaded attachments are written here. It may not be /tmp or another shared system directory, and there is no temp-directory fallback. FACE_CCTV_CAPTURE_DIRS none Extra absolute directories (colon-separated) in which a camera connection may name a local video file. The upload directory is always included. Any other local path is refused. FACE_TENANT default-tenant The instance’s tenant, and the only tenant variable FACE reads. It names the tenant sub-root tenants//, the tenant sessions carry, and the tenant the access page and subscription checks compare against. It does not name the connectors ConfigMap (see FACE_CONNECTORS_APP). Set it before the first boot (see Persistence). RUNNER_ID HOSTNAME On a runner, names its private tables. The face-runner manifest sets the stable value face-runner. FACE_CONNECTIONS_DIR none The legacy connection directory. It is imported once into the appfs root. FACE_DCI_CORPUS_DIR none An operator directory grounding also greps. FACE reads it and never writes to it. FACE’s own knowledge corpus is searched whether or not this is set. FETCH_LEDGER_DIR ./data/fetch-ledger The fetch cascade ledger. RALPH_RUN_DIR ./data/ralph-runs The agent run journal, used to resume runs. FACE_VOICE_SOURCE_DIR $RALPH_RUN_DIR/voice-sources Where recorded voice sources are written. RALPH_READ_ROOT . The root agents may read files under. Paths that escape it are rejected. FACE_DEPLOY_SECRETS_DIR none A directory of runner deploy secrets, read by path. EVIDENCE_FRAME_RETENTION 0 (none kept) How long camera evidence frames are kept, as a Go duration. It is capped at 720h. Litestream, outside the operator only. The image entrypoint runs the server under Litestream when MINIO_ENDPOINT is set, and /app/litestream.yml reads SQLITE_PATH, MINIO_ENDPOINT (host and port only, with no scheme), MINIO_BUCKET, MINIO_ACCESS_KEY and MINIO_SECRET_KEY. The operator sets none of them.

data: A deployment runs one FACE instance, managed by Runink TIDE, in the namespace face-system. This page lists the workloads in that namespace, says which ones the operator builds and which are plain manifests, and shows what to edit to change each one.
data.the-controlplane-resource#The \u003ccode:
face-operator owns the kind ControlPlane (API group runink.org/v1alpha1, short name cp). A deployment declares one, named face-control-plane.
Field Effect image The FACE backend image. replicas The pod count. The Deployment uses the Recreate strategy (see Upgrades). raftNodeId This control plane’s consensus node id, 1. tenant Becomes FACE_TENANT. Leave it empty: the operator then reads the tenant from the ConfigMap face-install-config, key FACE_TENANT. The reference is required, so a missing ConfigMap stops the pod instead of starting FACE on an empty tenant. The static face-runner reads the same key, so the two always agree. objectStoreEndpoint The object-store Service, as host:port. The default is face-objectd:9000. embeddingUrl Becomes EMBEDDING_URL, which FACE does not read. managedRunnerEndpoint Becomes MANAGED_RUNNER_ENDPOINT, the runner the control plane forwards fetches to. The deployment sets face-runner.face-system.svc:7102. scheduleExecuteFetch Sets SCHEDULE_EXECUTE_FETCH=true, so briefs run real fetches. ambassador The mTLS front door (mode: terminate, listenPort: 8443). With it on, FACE binds its app port to 127.0.0.1, the kubelet probes the health port 7101, and the Service carries only the mTLS and raft ports. probes Tunes the kubelet probes (see Health and troubleshooting). resources The backend container’s requests and limits. Unset, the operator uses CPU request 2 and limit 4, memory request 256Mi and limit 4Gi. tmp An emptyDir at /tmp with the given sizeLimit, for headless Chrome. env Extra environment variables. They are appended after the operator’s own list, so a literal here overrides the operator’s value of the same name. TIDE_PLATFORM_ADMIN, FACE_TENANT and the default FACE_APPFS_DIR are appended after env, so env cannot override them. nodeSelector A hard pin to labelled nodes, on top of the operator’s default placement. The operator also accepts a FaceInstance kind (a per-tenant runner). The deployment declares none: fetches run on the static face-runner.
A further kind, ClientInstance (core.runink.org/v1alpha1), belongs to TIDE’s operator. It records an instance’s app, tenant, image, users and subscription. FACE’s instance picker lists the ClientInstances whose spec.app matches RUNINK_APP (default face). The pod’s ServiceAccount needs list on clientinstances.core.runink.org for this.
data.the-frontend#The frontend:
face-frontend is a small static Go server in a distroless image. It serves /web and forwards a request to BACKEND_ADDR when the request is one of these:
a gRPC-web request; a request under /auth/, /api/ or /webrtc/; a dotted gRPC service path. In the deployment, BACKEND_ADDR is http://127.0.0.1:8081: an ambassador sidecar in the same pod (mode: originate) carries the call to face-control-plane on port 8443 over mTLS. The web app’s config.json (the sign-in client id) comes from the ConfigMap face-frontend-config, which tide wizard writes.
The release web build bakes in no backend host. The FACE app takes its origin from the page it was loaded from, so one bundle works behind any hostname.
Variable Default Purpose PORT 8080 The listen port. WEB_DIR /web The Flutter bundle directory. BACKEND_ADDR http://face-control-plane:7100 Where backend calls are forwarded.
data.the-static-runner#The static runner: face-runner runs the same image as SERVICE_ROLE=runner on port 7102, with RUNNER_ID=face-runner so its state survives restarts. It reads FACE_TENANT from face-install-config, uses the same object-store keys, KEK, session key and mesh CA as the control plane, and calls the model plane through TIDE’s model router. It does not set RAFT_NODE_ID, because runners are not consensus voters. The control plane reaches it over mesh mTLS.
data.the-workloads#The workloads:
Workload Role Built by Ports face-control-plane SERVICE_ROLE=server. It serves the FACE app’s gRPC-web and gRPC API, holds sessions and metadata, runs briefs and self-healing, and forwards every fetch to a runner. It never runs a fetch itself. face-operator, from the ControlPlane resource face-control-plane app 7100 (loopback only), health 7101, raft 7443, mTLS front door 8443 face-runner SERVICE_ROLE=runner. It runs the fetch pipeline (connectors, derivations, agents). Static manifest in TIDE’s on-host bundle 7102 face-frontend Serves the Flutter web bundle and forwards backend calls to the control plane. Static manifest in TIDE’s on-host bundle 8080 (Service port 80) objectd The object store FACE’s data lives in. Service face-objectd:9000. TIDE manifest 9000 face-operator Reconciles the ControlPlane resource into the control-plane Deployment and Service. TIDE manifest none The control plane and the runner use the same face-backend image. Only the role differs. TLS for browsers ends at the platform edge in front of these workloads. FACE itself has no browser certificate to configure.
The operator is the source of truth for the control-plane pod. If you edit the face-control-plane Deployment, the operator reconciles your change away. Edit the ControlPlane resource instead, usually its env list. The static workloads (face-runner, face-frontend) are not reconciled by any operator: change them in TIDE’s on-host bundle.
data.what-the-operator-puts-in-the-control-pl:
Containers
face-backend runs /app/server serve --port 7100. ambassador, the mTLS front door, when spec.ambassador enables it. It admits only a client certificate that chains to the mesh CA. Init containers, in this order:
connections-perms and raft-perms prepare the connections and raft volumes. The connections directory is made owner-only (mode 0700). ensure-bucket runs /app/server ensure-bucket. Volumes
Mount Kind Holds /data emptyDir Scratch only, such as uploads and the ingest spool. No database lives here. /raft node-local hostPath Consensus state (RAFT_DATA_DIR). /connections node-local hostPath The legacy connection layout (FACE_CONNECTIONS_DIR), imported once into the appfs root. /etc/face-runner-ca Secret face-control-plane-runner-ca The data-runner CA (FACE_RUNNER_CA_DIR), minted once by the operator and never rotated. Environment. The operator sets the role, port, raft settings, inference URLs, object-store settings and admission defaults (FACE_ADMIT_MAX=1, FACE_ADMIT_QUEUE=32). It also references these Secrets:
Secret Keys Required on the pod Created by the operator face-session AUTH_JWT_SECRET yes yes, if it is absent. It is never rotated on reconcile. tide-envelope-kek TIDE_ENVELOPE_KEK yes yes, if it is absent. It is never overwritten. tide-mesh-ca MESH_CA_CERT, MESH_CA_KEY yes no. You distribute it with tide mesh ca --namespace face-system. face-control-plane-admin email, password yes yes. It holds the break-glass admin as ADMIN_EMAIL and ADMIN_PASSWORD. objectd-key-face-app, objectd-key-face-vacuum access-key, secret-key yes, once they exist by TIDE’s provisioner. Until they exist, the pod uses the shared objectstore-creds pair. face-oauth google-client-id, oidc-issuer, allowed-emails, seed-users optional no face-recaptcha site-key, hostnames, secret-key optional no license LICENSE, LICENSE_PUBLIC_KEY optional no. You mint it with TIDE’s license tool. A required reference to a missing Secret or ConfigMap stops the pod before FACE runs. Kubernetes reports it as CreateContainerConfigError and names the object, so the cause shows up in kubectl describe pod and not in an application log.

data: All of FACE’s reasoning runs on a model plane inside the deployment’s own cluster: text generation, vision grading, and every agent (rules, posture, twins, compliance, the fetch cascade). FACE is an HTTP client of that plane. It ships no inference binary, starts no model process and has no local fallback. Runink TIDE runs the plane. mistral.rs is the intended engine, but nothing in FACE’s client is specific to mistral.rs.
data.check-the-boot-log#Check the boot log:
A healthy start logs:
🧭 Routing reasoning to the shared inference plane at (no local model server)
data.prove-the-plane-answers-through-face#Pro:
The boot check only proves that a URL is set. To prove that a model answers, sign in and call ModelService/Generate through FACE itself:
TOK=$(grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"method":"AUTH_METHOD_CREDENTIALS","username":"'"$ADMIN_EMAIL"'","password":"'"$ADMIN_PASSWORD"'"}' \ 127.0.0.1:$PORT semantics.v1.IdentityService/Login | grep -o '"token": "[^"]*"' | cut -d'"' -f4) test -n "$TOK" || echo "LOGIN RETURNED NO TOKEN" grpcurl -plaintext -H "authorization: Bearer $TOK" \ -d '{"prompt":"Say hello in one sentence.","temperature":0,"max_tokens":40}' \ 127.0.0.1:$PORT semantics.v1.ModelService/Generate A reply with model text and "finishReason": "stop" means the whole path works. In a cluster, run this against a kubectl port-forward to the pod’s app port. The login field is token. If that field comes back empty, the next call fails with invalid or expired session token, and the error points at the wrong call.
data.set-the-endpoint-variables#Set the endpo: export INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL='http://127.0.0.1:' In a cluster you do not set them by hand. The operator sets them on the control plane, and face-runner’s manifest sets them on the runner. INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL and VISION_REMOTE_URL point at TIDE’s model router (model-router.inference-system), and VOICE_REMOTE_URL at inference-voice.inference-system.
data.start-an-openai-compatible-server#Start: In a cluster, TIDE’s inference manifests provide the plane. Use the Service URL TIDE gives you. For a local run, any OpenAI-compatible server serving a chat model works.
data.the-contract#The contract:
The plane must speak the OpenAI-compatible HTTP API:
Call Request Notes Chat POST /v1/chat/completions Always sent with "stream": true. FACE reads server-sent events. Auth Authorization: Bearer Sent only when INFERENCE_API_KEY is non-empty. The model field carries a task id, not a file name: default for general reasoning, coder for code tasks and vision for vision tasks. A router in front of the engines can use this id to send each task to the right tier. Vision and voice calls go to VISION_REMOTE_URL and VOICE_REMOTE_URL. Both default to INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL.
FACE makes no embedding call. Its retrieval is grep over plain text, so the plane needs no embedding model for FACE. See Grounding.
data.what-each-failure-looks-like#What each f: Situation What you see INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL unset The process exits at boot with no inference endpoint configured: INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL is unset or blank. An endpoint was never configured for one call path That RPC fails with FailedPrecondition: is unavailable: no inference endpoint configured (INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL is unset or blank)… The plane requires a token and INFERENCE_API_KEY is empty An HTTP 401 on each call. It is not a boot failure. The plane is reachable but the model is still loading, or the model id is not served A per-call error from the plane. The boot check does not catch it.

data:
FACE keeps its state on self-hosted storage inside the deployment’s own cluster. There is no managed cloud database. Every store below is sealed at rest under keys derived from one platform key-encryption key, TIDE_ENVELOPE_KEK. That makes the KEK the most important thing to back up (see Key custody).
Store What it holds Where it lives appfs root Sessions, accounts, connections and their credentials, application metadata, fetch results, briefs, rule policies, compute budgets The object-store bucket FACE_APPFS_BUCKET (default face), or an encrypted local directory Control-plane state The application-metadata snapshot and boot marker, in an appfs table (kv) — the same table runners use The appfs root (object store, or the encrypted local directory) Record store Session traces (with clustering feature vectors) and feedback, as self-describing Avro The object store Knowledge corpus Plain-text passages per tenant, searched by grep (no vector index) The object store, under dci/knowledge//, or /knowledge/; a greppable copy is rebuilt in /dci-knowledge/ at start-up Camera evidence Evidence frames, when EVIDENCE_FRAME_RETENTION is set The object store Fetch ledger The fetch cascade’s ledger FETCH_LEDGER_DIR on local disk
data.credential-store#Credential store:
A connection’s credentials never sit in an environment variable or in the connection record. The connection record has no field a secret would fit in. When a connection is saved, secret-named fields are lifted into a credential bundle. Bundles are stored as rows of the tenant table tenants//var/lib/connections (credentials/), sealed under FACE’s derived key and bound to their path. Consensus replicates only the connection metadata snapshot, never the credentials.
Where FACE writes to local disk (the local appfs root, the knowledge corpus without an object store), directories are created 0700 and files 0600. The older layout (FACE_CONNECTIONS_DIR, with connections.json and credentials/*.json) is imported once on a persistent root, and each imported file is renamed .migrated.
data.key-custody#Key custody:
TIDE_ENVELOPE_KEK is a base64-encoded 32-byte key held in the tide-envelope-kek Secret in face-system. face-operator creates it if it is absent, and never rotates or overwrites it.
Losing the KEK loses the data. The whole appfs root (sessions, accounts, connection credentials, metadata), the sealed object-store objects and the knowledge snapshots cannot be decrypted without it. No recovery path exists, by design. Export the Secret to your offline key escrow as soon as it is created. Back it up separately from the data it protects. To change keys, keep the old key readable. TIDE_ENVELOPE_KEK_RETIRED takes a list of earlier KEKs (base64, separated by commas or whitespace). FACE and the storage libraries use them for decryption only, and seal new writes under TIDE_ENVELOPE_KEK. If you replace the KEK without listing the old one as retired, everything sealed under the old key becomes unreadable.
data.migrations-leave-a-rollback-in-place#Mig:
Each move to a new storage layout copies the data once and leaves the old copy behind, so you can go back to an older image:
Legacy metadata files are imported once into their table. Each one is then replaced by an envelope-sealed .migrated. To read one back:
go run -C grpc ./cmd/faceops metalog-unseal --table .migrated Older object-store tables (tables/face// in the object store’s own bucket) are copied into the appfs root on first open, and only into a table that has never been written. The originals are left in place.
The retired vector corpus (comet/ in the object store) is not read or migrated. It is left in place, untouched. Re-run document ingestion to make documents searchable in the knowledge corpus.
data.no-sqlite-database#No SQLite database:
FACE keeps no state in SQLite. The control plane’s application-metadata snapshot lives in an appfs table, like a runner’s state, sealed under FACE’s key in the object store. The operator runs no Litestream restore or replication, and the control plane’s /data volume is scratch only.
An instance upgraded from an earlier build may still have face.db at SQLITE_PATH. On boot, FACE opens it only if it exists (it never creates one), imports its rows once (the snapshot only when the appfs table has none, plus the legacy session revocations and connections), and never writes to it again. The file is left untouched as the rollback.
The image still bundles Litestream 0.5.17 and /app/litestream.yml. Only the image entrypoint uses them, when the image runs outside the operator with MINIO_ENDPOINT set:
litestream: restoring /app/grpc/data/face.db from MinIO (if a replica exists)... litestream: replicating /app/grpc/data/face.db -> MinIO; launching server... If MINIO_ENDPOINT is unset, it prints Litestream/MinIO not configured — running server without WAL replication. A failed restore stops the container with litestream restore failed: .
data.the-appfs-root#The appfs root:
At boot, FACE mounts its own application root, and it will not serve without it. When OBJECTSTORE_ENDPOINT is set, the root is the bucket FACE_APPFS_BUCKET (default face) on the object store. Otherwise, it is an encrypted local directory, FACE_APPFS_DIR. The root’s key is derived from the KEK for FACE alone, and every block is bound to its full path, so a sealed block cannot be moved to another path and still open. The boot log says which backend is in use:
🗂️ FACE appfs root online: objectstore bucket face, tenant 🗂️ FACE appfs root online: encrypted local directory /face, tenant The root is split into two scopes:
Deployment-wide: sessions (run/sessions), accounts (var/lib/auth_users) and compute budgets. Per tenant (tenants//, from the face-install-config ConfigMap in a deployment, default-tenant when unset): connections and their credentials, application metadata, the four fetch snapshots, briefs, remediation overlays and routes, rule policies and support calls. A runner gets its own tables at tenants//var/lib/runners... The exception is the fetch snapshots, which the runner writes and the control plane reads. That shared location is why a runner and its control plane must use the same tenant.
Set FACE_TENANT before an instance’s first boot. That boot copies any legacy data into the tenant it sees, once. If you set the tenant later, the legacy data stays under default-tenant. On a runner, keep RUNNER_ID stable. The operator uses the Deployment name. If it fell back to the pod name, every restart would start the runner on a fresh, empty set of tables. When there is no object store, the local root must be on storage that survives a restart. The operator points FACE_APPFS_DIR at appfs/ inside the pod’s persistent connections volume. If the default location next to face.db were used instead, it would be on the /data emptyDir, and sessions and credentials would be lost on every restart.
Sessions are validated on every request against this root, with a 2-second cache. A revocation on the control plane therefore takes effect on a runner within that window.
data.what-to-back-up#What to back up: The tide-envelope-kek Secret, escrowed offline. The face-install-config ConfigMap, which names the tenant the data is filed under. The object-store buckets FACE writes to on objectd: the face appfs bucket and the bucket in OBJECTSTORE_BUCKET. When there is no object store: the node-local connections volume, which contains the appfs root, and the knowledge directory. The node-local /raft volume, which holds the control plane’s consensus state (RAFT_DATA_DIR). To restore, put the KEK Secret and the tenant ConfigMap back first, then the object-store data, and only then start the control plane.

data:
FACE has five boot-time requirements. The order they are satisfied in matters. Each one must be present in the face-system namespace before you roll an image that requires it. If the image goes first, the pod crashloops instead of starting. A crashloop is the designed outcome, because an operator sees it within the first minute. Still, it is an outage you can avoid by landing the deployment side first.
Requirement Supplied as Where it comes from Session signing key AUTH_JWT_SECRET The face-session Secret. face-operator creates it if it is absent. Shared mesh CA MESH_CA_CERT, MESH_CA_KEY The tide-mesh-ca Secret, distributed with tide mesh ca --namespace face-system. At-rest key encryption key (KEK) TIDE_ENVELOPE_KEK The tide-envelope-kek Secret. The operator creates it if it is absent and never overwrites it. Tenant FACE_TENANT The ConfigMap face-install-config, key FACE_TENANT. Both the control plane and face-runner read it, and neither starts without it. Inference endpoint INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL Set by the operator on the control plane and in face-runner’s manifest. The three secrets are read through the platform secret backend (SECRET_BACKEND). With the default env backend, they come from the environment. With SECRET_BACKEND=file, they come from files in SECRETS_DIR (default /var/run/secrets), and the environment is the fallback. A file may be named exactly like the variable (AUTH_JWT_SECRET) or in lower case with dashes (auth-jwt-secret).
data.confirm-the-inference-endpoint#Confirm t: kubectl -n face-system set env deploy/face-control-plane --list | grep INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL kubectl -n face-system set env deploy/face-runner --list | grep INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL Then prove the endpoint answers. See Model plane.
data.confirm-the-kek-and-session-secrets#Conf: kubectl -n face-system get secret tide-envelope-kek face-session When the operator reconciles a ControlPlane, it creates both Secrets if they are missing. If you provision them yourself, the KEK must be a base64-encoded 32-byte key (openssl rand -base64 32). Escrow the KEK before any data is written. See Persistence and backup.
data.confirm-the-tenant#Confirm the tenant: kubectl -n face-system get configmap face-install-config -o jsonpath='{.data.FACE_TENANT}' The tenant keys the data (tenants//). Create the ConfigMap before the first boot, and do not change it afterwards.
data.distribute-the-mesh-ca#Distribute the me: tide mesh ca --namespace face-system kubectl -n face-system get secret tide-mesh-ca -o jsonpath='{.data.MESH_CA_CERT}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates The Secret needs both keys, and the CA must be inside its validity window. An expired CA fails the same way a missing one does, and restarting the pod does not help: redistribute the CA first.
data.roll-the-image#Roll the image: Only now roll the FACE image. See Upgrades and CD.
data.the-fatal-at-boot-checks#The fatal-at-bo:
These checks run in runServer in the order shown. Each one ends the process with the message quoted, followed by guidance text that is not reproduced here.
1. Session signing key. This runs first, before the port is bound.
❌ refusing to serve: face has no session signing key configured (AUTH_JWT_SECRET unset) There is deliberately no generated fallback. A generated key would differ per replica, so users would be signed out whenever a request reached another pod. Outside a cluster, set AUTH_JWT_SECRET directly.
2. Mesh identity.
❌ mesh identity unavailable, refusing to start: MESH_CA_CERT: secret "MESH_CA_CERT" is not configured The same line names MESH_CA_KEY when that key is the one missing, and carries the CA loader’s error when the CA is unusable. The mesh planes (control plane to runner, raft peers, the mTLS half of the app port) are only ever served over mTLS. No setting of any variable turns this check off.
3. Inference endpoint.
no inference endpoint configured: INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL is unset or blank. FACE ships no inference binary and has no local fallback tier. This check only proves that a value is set. It does not prove that the plane is reachable, or that a model is loaded.
4. The appfs root. This is where sessions live, so FACE will not serve without it.
FACE appfs root: … envelope: at-rest KEK unavailable: TIDE_ENVELOPE_KEK: secret "TIDE_ENVELOPE_KEK" is not configured When this line appears, confirm the encryption key is configured for the instance.
The wrapped part depends on the backend. With no object store it is appfs: refusing to mount without at-rest encryption:. With an object store it starts approot: object store configured but unavailable:. The line always starts FACE appfs root: and always ends with the KEK error.
For any other mount failure, including an object store that is configured but unavailable, the message is:
❌ FACE appfs root could not be mounted (refusing to serve without its session store): 5. The state table. FACE opens its state table in the appfs root: ❌ control-plane state table: on the control plane, ❌ runner state table: on a runner. On a control plane upgraded from an earlier build, a leftover face.db is read once. A missing KEK there is fatal and the message starts with Legacy face.db:. Any other failure to read it is logged and retried at the next boot.
6. Later services. The process also stops if one of these fails:
ConfigService: ❌ Failed to init ConfigService (refusing to serve without it — connections, runners, integrations and SQL credentials all resolve through this store) IdentityService: ❌ Failed to init IdentityService (refusing to serve without authentication) mounting the shared UI components: ❌ ui comms, ❌ ui rulesrecon, ❌ ui estate, ❌ ui datasources, ❌ ui billing, ❌ ui siteplan, ❌ ui profile, ❌ ui access, ❌ ui voice starting the raft orchestrator while RAFT_NODE_ID is set: raft orchestrator failed to start and RAFT_NODE_ID= is set, so this pod is a configured voting member on a runner, RUNNER_ENROLL_ADDR is set but RUNNER_ENROLL_TOKEN is not (see Runners). The object store refuses to start without credentials: objectstore: refusing to start without credentials. It also refuses if the removed variable OBJECTSTORE_USE_SSL is still set. Put the scheme in OBJECTSTORE_ENDPOINT instead (https://host:port).
In a cluster, a missing required Secret shows up before any of these log lines, as CreateContainerConfigError on the pod. The references to face-session, tide-envelope-kek, tide-mesh-ca and face-install-config are required on purpose, so that the failure names the missing object.

data:
A fetch runs on a runner, never on the control plane. The control plane receives RunFetch, forwards it to a runner together with the caller’s session and the connection credentials the fetch needs, and streams the runner’s progress back to the FACE app. At startup each process logs which role it has:
🧵 Fetch role: CONTROL-PLANE — forwards fetches to the dedicated runner at (never runs them here). 🧵 Fetch role: RUNNER — executes the fetch pipeline in-process (dedicated compute). A runner is the FACE backend image started with SERVICE_ROLE=runner. Every boot check on Prerequisites and ordering applies to a runner as well, including the mesh CA, the KEK and the inference endpoint. A runner also mounts the same appfs root as its control plane, because it validates the forwarded session there and writes its fetch results there.
How to connect data sources to runners, and how to choose a runner for a source, is covered in Data sources. This page covers operating the runners themselves.
data.deploying-runners-from-face#Deploying ru:
An organisation admin can deploy, redeploy and decommission a runner from Settings › Integrations › Runners. Any other role, and any service account, is refused, and nothing is deployed. Every attempt is audited, and deployment records survive a restart.
Target What FACE does Needs On premises Copies the runner image archive or binary this server holds to your machine over SSH, checked against its SHA-256. FACE_RUNNER_IMAGE_ARCHIVE with FACE_RUNNER_IMAGE_ARCHIVE_SHA256 (and FACE_RUNNER_IMAGE_REF), or FACE_RUNNER_BINARY with FACE_RUNNER_BINARY_SHA256. Google Cloud Starts a Compute Engine VM in your project from an image in your registry. No service-account JSON key is used, and Cloud Run is refused. FACE_RUNNER_GCP_IMAGE, a digest-pinned image. Snowflake, Databricks Starts a runner that connects out to FACE’s runner channel over mutual TLS. FACE_RUNNER_CHANNEL_ADDR and FACE_RUNNER_CHANNEL_LISTEN, and the runner CA in FACE_RUNNER_CA_DIR. Without them the targets are listed as unavailable. Deploy credentials come from the connection’s sealed credentials and non-secret settings, and from files under FACE_DEPLOY_SECRETS_DIR, read by path. See Plans and billing for how runners in your own cloud are charged on the Dedicated plan.
data.self-hosted-runners-outbound-enrolment#S:
A self-hosted runner runs on your own machine and dials out to the control plane. Nothing dials in to it. The runner authenticates with a service-account token issued for your tenant by IdentityService.GenerateServiceAccountKey, holds one enrolment stream open, and runs the fetches the control plane assigns over that stream.
Variable Purpose SERVICE_ROLE=runner Starts the process as a runner. RUNNER_ENROLL_ADDR The control plane’s gRPC address, as seen from the runner. Setting it turns enrolment on. RUNNER_ENROLL_TOKEN The service-account token. It is required. RUNNER_ID A stable id, so that a reconnect takes the same registry slot. RUNNER_NAME, RUNNER_VERSION Shown in the control plane’s runner registry. RUNNER_ENROLL_TLS Defaults to TLS with the system roots. When enrolment starts, the runner logs:
🛰️ Outbound runner enrolment enabled: dialling (runner id "") If RUNNER_ENROLL_ADDR is set without a token, the runner refuses to start:
❌ RUNNER_ENROLL_ADDR is set but RUNNER_ENROLL_TOKEN is empty — a runner enrols with a service-account token issued by IdentityService.GenerateServiceAccountKey; there is no anonymous enrolment When the stream ends, the runner reconnects after 5 seconds.
An enrolled runner handles one kind of work, fetch. It does not persist, queue or retry work. A fetch assigned while the runner is shutting down is lost, and the control plane sees a deadline. Rotate the service-account token the way you rotate any credential, then restart the runner with the new value. You can start self-hosted runners yourself, as above, or deploy them from Settings › Integrations › Runners (below).
data.snowflake-runners#Snowflake runners: runink runner create provisions a Snowflake Container Services runner. It reads --compute-pool (or RUNNER_COMPUTE_POOL, which is required for that type), RUNNER_CPU_LIMIT (default 1) and RUNNER_MEMORY_LIMIT (default 1G). It stops if the compute pool is not named, because it cannot invent one.
data.the-in-cluster-runner#The in-cluster run:
A deployment has one in-cluster runner: the static face-runner Deployment in face-system, from Runink TIDE’s on-host bundle. The control plane dials it at MANAGED_RUNNER_ENDPOINT (face-runner.face-system.svc:7102) over mutual TLS from the shared mesh CA. It never falls back to plaintext.
Task How Size the runner Change the requests and limits in face-runner’s manifest in TIDE’s on-host bundle. No operator reconciles it. Point the control plane at a runner spec.managedRunnerEndpoint on the ControlPlane resource face-control-plane. Refuse to run fetch work on the control plane Set REQUIRE_RUNNER_ISOLATION=true in the ControlPlane env. An unreachable runner is then a hard failure. Keep runner state across restarts Keep RUNNER_ID stable. The manifest sets face-runner. Keep runner and control plane on one tenant Both read FACE_TENANT from the face-install-config ConfigMap. Do not set it anywhere else. Runners are not consensus voters. They leave RAFT_NODE_ID and RAFT_MTLS_ADDR unset, and a runner’s /readyz reports the raft check as skipped. That is expected: the control plane is the only voting member.
When a runner cannot be reached, the fetch fails with:
Analysis failed: dedicated runner unreachable — fetch does not run on the control plane: explains the dial error. Look for a runner pod that is not Ready, an endpoint that points at the wrong Service, or a mesh certificate that no longer chains to the CA the control plane holds.

data.a-change-does-not-stick-or-a-roll-change: A config change is reverted. You edited the live Deployment, and the operator reconciled it back. Change the ControlPlane resource’s env instead. A value in env is ignored. Some names are appended after env. TIDE_PLATFORM_ADMIN and FACE_TENANT always win. Same image digest after the roll. The build did not reach the registry, or the commit produced an identical image. Pin the digest to be sure what is running. RAFT_DATA_DIR unset — raft state is MEMORY-ONLY. This is fine for local development. In a cluster, the operator sets it to /raft.
data.grounding-finds-nothing#Grounding finds: Retrieval is a word match, not a meaning match (see Grounding). A passage is found only when it shares words with the question. Check that the documents were ingested: Why lists the documents behind the business rules. Then ask with the words the documents use. No model or embedding setting affects retrieval.
data.health-endpoints#Health endpoints:
The backend serves three unauthenticated HTTP endpoints on its app port, 7100 on the control plane and 7102 on a runner. Behind the mTLS ambassador the control plane’s app port listens on 127.0.0.1 only, so it serves these three paths, and nothing else, on the health port 7101 as well. The kubelet probes that port.
Path Answers Use it for GET /livez Always 200 with "status": "alive", once the process has reached its serving loop. It checks no shared dependency. Liveness. A fleet-wide failure then does not restart every pod at once. GET /readyz 200 ready or 503 not_ready, with one entry per check. Readiness. When it fails, the pod is taken out of rotation but stays alive to be inspected. GET /auth/config The FACE app’s sign-in configuration. The operator’s default probe path. It answers once the web handler is serving. /readyz evaluates two checks:
mesh_identity fails when the rotating mesh leaf is unhealthy, or does not chain to the loaded CA. Track the mesh CA’s expiry: an expired CA stops every mesh connection. raft_consensus is evaluated only on a consensus member (RAFT_NODE_ID set). It fails when the member has had no leader for longer than a 30-second grace period, or when the raft loop does not answer a status query. On a runner it is skipped. kubectl -n face-system port-forward deploy/face-control-plane 7100:7100 & curl -s localhost:7100/readyz | jq
data.kubelet-probes#Kubelet probes:
The operator puts startup, readiness and liveness probes on the backend container. Tune them under spec.probes of the ControlPlane resource. The static face-runner carries its own probes in its manifest.
Field Default path /auth/config. It is used by all three probes, and it is always the startup probe’s path. readinessPath, livenessPath path startupSeconds 900. This is the boot budget before the kubelet restarts the container. Probes run every 10 seconds. readinessFailureThreshold, livenessFailureThreshold 3, 6. Liveness runs every 30 seconds. timeoutSeconds 5 disabled false. It removes all three probes. To make readiness reflect the mesh and consensus, set readinessPath: /readyz and livenessPath: /livez. Do not point the startup probe or the liveness probe at /readyz. A shared failure, such as an expired CA, would then restart every pod and destroy the state you need to diagnose it.
data.running-but-panels-are-empty-or-say-noth:
FACE never fills a panel with data it did not read. An empty panel is either an empty estate or a stated failure. Work through these in order:
No data source. On Why, the domain graph answers connect a data source first, and posture answers no data sources to assess. A fetch with no connection selected fails with No data source was selected. Add a connection in Settings › Integrations › Systems (see Data sources), include it on Ask, and ask a question. The fetch never reached a runner. The fetch reports Analysis failed: dedicated runner unreachable — fetch does not run on the control plane:. Check the runner’s readiness and MANAGED_RUNNER_ENDPOINT. The model plane is not answering. The boot log shows the configured URL, but calls fail. Call ModelService/Generate as shown in Model plane. A FailedPrecondition that names INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL means one call path has no endpoint. Briefs produce nothing. Without SCHEDULE_EXECUTE_FETCH=true, each trigger logs 📅 scheduled trigger (dry-run): … — set SCHEDULE_EXECUTE_FETCH=true to run the real fetch. The instance picker says “Instance discovery is unavailable”. The pod could not list ClientInstances. Its ServiceAccount needs list on clientinstances.core.runink.org.
data.sign-in-fails#Sign-in fails: Message Cause invalid or expired session token The session was revoked or has expired, or the bearer token was empty. On runners: the runner does not share the control plane’s appfs root. Password sign-in is disabled — use Google sign-in AUTH_GOOGLE_ONLY=true. Sign in with Google. SSO is not available on this instance SSO is configured, but AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS is empty. The log line is sso_login_refused_no_allowlist. This account is not authorized for this instance The account is not in AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS. The operator projects the list from the face-oauth Secret (allowed-emails). The pod must restart to pick it up. OIDC not configured (set OIDC_ISSUER and OIDC_CLIENT_ID) SSO was attempted with no issuer or client id set. A Google token is rejected for its audience The FACE app’s google_client_id (in face-frontend-config) must equal OIDC_CLIENT_ID, or set OIDC_AUDIENCE. The admin cannot log in at all Look for break-glass admin not seeded: ADMIN_EMAIL and/or ADMIN_PASSWORD unset at boot. The operator takes both from the face-control-plane-admin Secret.
data.the-pod-crashloops#The pod crashloops:
Read the first lines of the previous container’s log:
kubectl -n face-system logs deploy/face-control-plane -c face-backend --previous | grep -m3 -E '❌|refusing|no inference endpoint|FACE appfs root|Legacy face.db' Log line starts with Cause and fix ❌ refusing to serve: face has no session signing key configured (AUTH_JWT_SECRET unset) The session key is missing. Provide face-session, or set AUTH_JWT_SECRET outside a cluster. ❌ mesh identity unavailable, refusing to start: The CA is missing, incomplete or expired. Check both keys and the validity dates, then redistribute with tide mesh ca --namespace face-system. Restarting does not fix an expired CA. no inference endpoint configured: INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL is unset or blank. Set INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL. The retired names REMOTE_LLAMA_URL and LLAMA_REMOTE_URL are not read. FACE appfs root: … at-rest KEK unavailable TIDE_ENVELOPE_KEK did not resolve. Check kubectl -n face-system get secret tide-envelope-kek. FACE appfs root: … envelope: TIDE_ENVELOPE_KEK is not valid base64 or KEK must be 32 bytes The key is malformed. Do not generate a new one if data already exists: restore the original from escrow. ❌ FACE appfs root could not be mounted … object store configured but unavailable The object store is unreachable, or the credentials are wrong. objectstore: refusing to send object-store traffic … means the endpoint needs https://. objectstore: OBJECTSTORE_USE_SSL is set Remove the variable, and put the scheme in OBJECTSTORE_ENDPOINT. raft orchestrator failed to start and RAFT_NODE_ID= is set Consensus state could not be opened. Often the previous pod still held its lock; the next restart usually clears it. If this pod is not meant to vote, unset RAFT_NODE_ID. ❌ RUNNER_ENROLL_ADDR is set but RUNNER_ENROLL_TOKEN is empty A self-hosted runner is missing its token (see Runners). SQLITE_PATH="…" must be an absolute path or PORT="…" is not a port number The image entrypoint rejected its input. This applies only when the image runs through /app/entrypoint, outside the operator.
data.the-pod-never-starts-createcontainerconf: A required Secret or ConfigMap is missing from face-system. kubectl describe pod names it. The usual ones are tide-mesh-ca, tide-envelope-kek, face-session and the face-install-config ConfigMap. Create or distribute it (see Prerequisites and ordering). The pod starts on its own at the next retry.

data.build#Build: The image is built with tag latest.
data.confirm#Confirm:
Compare the new digest with the old one. If they match, treat it as a warning, not a success: either the build never reached the registry, or the commit produced an identical image. A rollout that rolled nothing looks exactly like one that worked.
Rollouts through the operator use the Recreate strategy. The old pod stops and releases its storage lock before the new pod starts. Expect a few seconds of unavailability per roll. Do not change the strategy to rolling: two pods would contend for the same single-writer state.
data.continuous-delivery#Continuous delivery: A release is built, checked against the cluster, rolled, and then confirmed. These four steps are what a rollout does, whether Runink performs it for a managed deployment or you drive the same sequence yourself:
data.escrow-the-kek#Escrow the KEK: Confirm that the KEK is in escrow before you upgrade. Storage migrations run on first boot. See Persistence and backup.
data.image-references-and-pull-policy#Image r:
The operator pulls with Always for a tag, and with IfNotPresent for a digest (image@sha256:…). TIDE_IMAGE_PULL_POLICY on the operator overrides both. For production and air-gapped sites, pin the image field of the ControlPlane resource, and the images in the face-runner and face-frontend manifests, to a digest, so that every roll is reproducible and a rollback is exact.
When the tide-mesh-ca Secret changes, the operator writes its hash into the pod template annotation core.runink.org/mesh-ca-hash. The change rolls the pods, so each one picks up the new CA.
data.preflight#Preflight: Check that kubectl reaches the cluster (kubectl get --raw=/readyz). If it does not, stop and roll nothing — a rollout against an unreachable API server leaves you unable to tell a failed deploy from a failed connection.
data.read-the-releases-new-requirements#Read: If a release adds a boot requirement, the deployment side must land first: Prerequisites and ordering explains why. Check face-system for tide-mesh-ca, tide-envelope-kek, face-session and face-install-config, and check that INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL is set on both face-control-plane and face-runner.
data.remove-names-the-new-image-refuses#Remov: Take OBJECTSTORE_USE_SSL out of any env list. It is refused at startup. The full list of retired names is at the end of the Configuration reference.
data.roll#Roll: Record the running image digest, delete the pod, and wait up to 300 seconds for rollout status. A backend release rolls the control plane (face-control-plane) and the static face-runner; a frontend release rolls face-frontend.
data.roll-the-control-plane-then-the-runner#R: The control plane and runners must be able to verify each other’s mesh certificates, and they must agree on the tenant.
data.rolling-back#Rolling back: Storage migrations leave the old data in place: .migrated files, older object-store tables and the old knowledge index. See Migrations leave a rollback in place. So an older image can usually boot against the same stores, without anything written after the upgrade. Roll back by setting the ControlPlane image field, and the face-runner image, back to the previous digest. Do not roll back the KEK: the same KEK must stay in place.
data.the-images#The images:
FACE ships two images. Both are built from source by Runink and pushed to the cluster’s node-local registry.
Image Contents face-backend /app/server (the runink CLI; serve starts the backend), /app/entrypoint, Litestream 0.5.17 (SHA-256 pinned, used only by the entrypoint outside the operator), and a headless Chromium for rendering. It runs as a non-root user (uid 1000) on a pinned Debian slim base. face-frontend The release Flutter web bundle and the static sleeve, on a distroless base. Two properties of these builds matter to you as an operator. Neither image is assembled from prebuilt binaries — every release is compiled from source, and the protobuf stubs are regenerated during the build rather than carried along. And the frontend has no backend address compiled into it, so one image serves every deployment: you point it at your own control plane at run time, never at build time.
data.verify#Verify: Check that /readyz returns ready, that the grounding line reads ACTIVE, and that a ModelService/Generate call answers. See Health and troubleshooting.

data:
Runink FACE (Fulfilment Autonomous Claims Engine) takes the chasing out of logistics claims and exceptions. Today a shortage, a warm reefer or an overbilled accessorial is found by someone reading across the warehouse system, the telematics feed and the paperwork, often after the claim window has closed. FACE connects to the systems an operation already runs (warehouses, ERPs, telematics, sensors, cameras), finds those cases, and hands a person the answer, the evidence and the drafted decision to approve.
The models FACE reasons with run inside the platform FACE is deployed on: Runink’s shared machines on the Lite plan, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is called on any plan.
Start here if you are evaluating FACE, planning a deployment, or new to the vocabulary.
What FACE isThe journey: Ask, Briefs, Options, Why and Actionable Twins. ArchitectureThe components, where your data lives, and where it travels. ConceptsInstances, connections, runners, runs, personas, options, checks, decisions. Plans and billingLite, Dedicated and Enterprise; Compute Units, fees, currency.
data.where-to-go-next#Where to go next: If you are… Read An operator or analyst using FACE day to day Using FACE Connecting FACE to your systems Data sources Assessing how findings are produced Analysis & evidence A security or compliance reviewer Security & trust Deploying or running an instance Operating FACE Integrating programmatically gRPC API reference Choosing a plan or reading a bill Plans and billing

data:
FACE is application code that runs on the Runink platform: a Kubernetes cluster (k0s) managed by Runink TIDE. TIDE deploys FACE and supplies the shared services it relies on: the TLS edge, the inference plane, the service mesh’s certificate authority, the key that encrypts FACE’s data at rest, and the object store. Where the work runs depends on your plan; see Plans and billing.
FACE runs in its own namespace, face-system. Each deployment runs one FACE instance, which TIDE’s operator manages.
flowchart TB U[Browser: the FACE app] -->|HTTPS| E[Platform TLS edge] E --> FE[face-frontendserves the app, proxies its calls] FE -->|gRPC-web, same origin| CP[face-control-planegRPC services] subgraph ns [face-system namespace] FE CP R[face-runnermanaged runner] end CP -->|in-cluster HTTP| MP[Inference planetext · vision · voice] CP --> S[(Encrypted storageobject store · metadata · records)] CP -->|mutual TLS| R R --> DS[(Your data sources)] CP -->|mutual TLS| SR[Self-hosted runnerin your network] SR --> DS2[(Data sources behindyour firewall)]
data.components#Components: Component What it does face-frontend Serves the Flutter web app and passes its calls (gRPC-web, sign-in and API paths) to the control plane on the same origin, so the app needs no backend address baked in. face-control-plane The FACE gRPC backend: runs, briefs, analysis, options, the twins and their decisions, follow-ups, remediation, camera and sensor feeds, and the other services in the API reference. TIDE’s operator renders it from the instance’s FaceInstance resource. face-runner The managed runner: a FACE process that reads your data sources from inside the cluster. It is the default runner for every connection. Self-hosted runners Runners you run in your own network, so reads happen close to the data. A runner enrols with a single-use setup ticket, and FACE reaches it over mutual TLS on its own runner certificate authority. Inference plane The platform’s shared language, vision and voice models, behind an OpenAI-compatible HTTP interface. FACE ships no model server and refuses to start without the plane’s address. Storage FACE’s encrypted file tree on the platform object store (sessions, users, connections, schedules, run records), a metadata database with its values sealed, and append-only logs for traces and data lineage. Mesh The control plane’s peers replicate the connection registry over mutual TLS, with certificates from the platform’s certificate authority. Credentials never travel over the mesh.
data.instances-and-access#Instances and acces: An instance is defined on the platform as a ClientInstance resource that TIDE’s operator owns. It names the people who may use the instance and until when. When you sign in, FACE lists the instances you hold a grant on, read from those resources. It never shows an instance you may not use, and never invents one when the list cannot be read. See Sign in and choose an instance.
data.where-your-data-goes#Where your data goe: Model calls stay in the platform. Prompts, retrieved records and model outputs go only to the inference plane. Outbound calls go only to what you connect. That means your data sources, plus the web searches, messaging and email channels you configure. FACE calls no paid map or geocoding service. Credentials are separated from configuration. A connection record has no field that can hold a secret. Credentials go to a sealed credential store and are never returned through the API. At rest, data is encrypted under a key derived from the key-encryption key the platform provides. FACE refuses to start without it rather than fall back to plaintext. Details and limits are in Security & trust. Deployment and configuration are in Operating FACE.

data:
The terms below are used throughout the app, the API and these docs, in the order you meet them on the journey.
Term Meaning Instance One FACE deployment for one organisation, managed by Runink TIDE. After sign-in you choose the instance to work in; the list shows only the instances you hold a grant on. Connection A configured link to one data source: its type (for example Snowflake, SAP, MQTT or a camera) and its settings. Credentials are stored separately and are write-only. See Data sources. Runner The process that reads a data source. The managed runner is part of the server. Self-hosted runners run in your network and enrol with the instance. Test A connection check. It opens the source with its stored credential, read-only and time-limited, and reads nothing. A connector with no reachability check says so. Source backing Whether anything FACE ships stands behind a connection. LIVE means nothing of FACE’s stands in, so the connection reads whatever it addresses and a failure surfaces as a failure. Unspecified means the server did not compute it. Run One question asked of your data, on Ask or by a brief: FACE reads the sources, answers, then runs the analysis and the twins’ decisions in the background. The app calls it a fetch. Selected run The one run that Ask, Options, Why and Actionable Twins show. Pages never borrow figures from another run. Persona Who a run or a brief is for: a name, the question its brief asks, the money figure it reads first, and its plays. The product ships five; an instance can reword them or add its own. With none picked, a run uses the Generalist view. Play What FACE recovers or protects money on: claims recovery, disruptions, routes, fulfilment, cold chain, maintenance, inventory and fleet. Brief A question FACE asks on its own, at a set time or when data changes, for one persona, telling the people you choose what needs a decision. See Briefs. Option One way to act on a decision, scored on one shared measure with a range. FACE recommends an option only when it is a clear winner. See Options. Check A test FACE runs on the rows a run read, such as “Deliveries arrive by their promise”. It holds, fails, or is not measured. See Why. Rule A business rule FACE found in your systems or you added, checked against what your systems do and against your policy documents. Decision A drafted action (a claim, a dispute, an order, a route re-plan) waiting on Actionable Twins until a named person approves or rejects it. Lanes sort decisions into Waiting for you, In flight and Back. Evidence document A structured document FACE derives from your data, such as an OS&D report, a temperature-excursion record or a custody audit. The set of document kinds is fixed, and each is built only from the records it cites. Decision artifact The full record of one decision, with the drafts it would produce. Follow-up A flow that calls or messages the people responsible for an item, on rules you approve. It runs by itself only once armed. Remediation The work after a compliance, finance or operations finding: assign it, decide it and route it. Trace The recorded history of a run: its steps, the sources it read, and what it produced. Data lineage An append-only record of which source was read, when, with what shape and outcome. It records structure only, never the values returned. Grounding Retrieving your own records (Direct Corpus Interaction: lexical search over your own corpus, no embeddings) to support a model’s reasoning, so answers cite your data.

FACE is sold per seat, on one of three plans. The plans differ in where the work runs, and that decides how compute is charged. One outcome fee, for claims recovery, applies on top of the seats, and only on money confirmed as recovered.
data.compute-units#Compute Units:
1 CU is one second of holding a shared model slot, so 3,600 CU is one slot-hour.
The model router measures it, on every model call FACE makes, and FACE records the exact milliseconds. The milliseconds are summed over the billing period and converted to CU once, rounded up. A call the router did not measure is not charged. It is counted as a gap and logged. CU is charged only on Lite, where the work runs on Runink’s hardware. Dedicated and Enterprise are never charged CU overage. A run has no fixed CU price. What a run costs is the model time it used. The dedicated CUs you set under Settings › Subscription are a separate control, not the plan’s allowance (see Compute units).
data.currency-and-billing-periods#Currency an: One price list, in US dollars. A bill is stated in your regional currency, converted at the European Central Bank euro reference rate in force when the month opens: the last publication before the 1st, fixed for the whole month. Seat prices round to a whole unit of the local currency, and usage and fees to its smallest unit. A missing or stale rate stops the bill. It is never guessed and never 0. Anniversary periods. A billing period runs from your subscription’s start date, not the calendar month.
data.outcome-fee#Outcome fee:
Fee Amount When it applies Claims recovery 20% of what is recovered Only on money confirmed as recovered. Nothing is charged when nothing is recovered. The fee follows only from a confirmed recovery. The type or wording of a decision, a model’s output and a client request field can’t select or trigger it. A claims-recovery fee is never computed from what a document asks for, from an insurer’s reserve or from a filed claim.
Approving a decision charges no fee. The claims-recovery fee follows only from money confirmed as recovered.
data.plans#Plans: Plan Where the work runs Price Seats Compute Units (CU) Lite Runink’s shared capacity, spot-style $75 per seat per month, billed yearly, or $89 per seat month to month 1 to 9 18,000 CU per seat per month, pooled across the account’s seats. Beyond that, $0.10 per 100 CU. Dedicated Runners in your own cloud account: Google Cloud (Compute Engine), Databricks or Snowflake $149 per seat per month, billed yearly 10 or more Unlimited, never charged as overage. A runner fee of 1% of those runners’ cloud cost applies. There is no node fee. Enterprise Your premises or your own cloud account Custom quote 10 or more Unlimited, never charged as overage. On-premises runners carry no runner fee. On Dedicated, the runners’ cloud cost itself is on your cloud provider’s bill, not on Runink’s. The 1% runner fee is the only compute line Runink adds.
data.where-you-see-it-in-face#Where you see i: The subscription (plan, seats and status) is set by the platform operator on the instance and shown under Settings › Subscription. FACE takes no payment itself. Settings › Subscription shows plans and prices for reference, and checkout is disabled there. Readers and service accounts can’t start a checkout or open the billing portal. A figure FACE did not measure is shown as Not measured, never as 0 or $0.00.
data.who-is-charged-for-usage#Who is charged:
Model time is charged to the billing account of the purchaser who made the call. FACE resolves that account on the server from the verified session: the signed-in user, then that user’s purchaser in the account file the platform operator provides (RUNINK_ACCOUNTS_FILE). This holds on an instance several purchasers share: each purchaser’s usage is recorded against their own account, never the instance’s.
A request field or a model’s output never chooses the account. A service account’s calls and the platform’s own work are never billed. A user no purchaser has placed is recorded as unattributed and logged. The usage is not billed to another account and does not disappear.

data:
Runink FACE (Fulfilment Autonomous Claims Engine) is for the people who chase logistics losses: claims, cold-chain excursions, customs holds, deductions and invoice disputes. Instead of reading across systems by hand to build each case, they ask FACE a question, get the answer with the money at stake, and decide what happens next. Every figure is cited to the record it came from.
FACE reasons over an organisation’s own operational data and turns it into decisions a person reviews, approves and acts on. It is a Go gRPC backend and a Flutter web app.
data.principles-you-can-rely-on#Principles yo: Sovereign AI. Every model call goes to the inference plane of your deployment: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. FACE sends your data to no outside AI service on any plan. Your data stays yours. Connection credentials are sealed and never returned by the API. Data at rest is encrypted, and FACE refuses to start without its encryption key. See Security & trust. Honest outputs. “Not measured” and “could not be read” are different things, and neither is ever shown as zero. A document is produced only when the evidence supports it. FACE never acts alone. Every decision waits until a named person approves or rejects it, and FACE recommends an option only when it is a clear winner. A decision is stored with the authenticated identity of the person who made it.
data.the-journey-ask--briefs--options--why--a: flowchart LR A[Aska question, the answer first] --> B[Briefsthe same questions, on a schedule] A --> C[Optionswhat could we do] B --> C C --> D[Whythe checks and rules behind it] D --> E[Actionable Twinsapprove, reject, follow up] E -->|approved| F[Your systems and people] Ask. You ask a question of your connected systems, by typing, speaking or attaching files. FACE reads your sources through a connection, either directly or through a runner you control, and answers first: what it found, what is owed and at risk, and how many decisions wait for you. See Ask. Briefs. The questions each persona cares about are asked for you, every week or when your data changes, and the people responsible are told what needs a decision. See Briefs. Options. For each decision the run’s checks stand behind, FACE compares the options on one measure and recommends one only when it is a clear winner. See Options. Why. Every check FACE ran on the rows it read, what your records and public pages say about each counterparty, and the business rules behind them. See Why. Actionable Twins. The digital twins draft the decisions: claims, disputes, orders, route re-plans. Each waits for a named person to approve or reject it, and follow-ups chase what comes back. See Actionable Twins. Behind each run, records are grouped into data domains and kept as plain text that FACE searches and reads directly (Direct Corpus Interaction: no embeddings, no vector index), so its reasoning is grounded in your records rather than in a model’s general knowledge. Language and vision models served inside the platform work alongside classical statistics and machine learning. See Analysis & evidence.
data.what-it-is-used-for#What it is used for:
FACE recovers or protects money on a set of plays, claims first:
Claims recovery. Cross-checking deliveries, weights and counts against shipping documents, watching claim windows, and drafting the claim and its evidence. Disruptions and routes. Late or short shipments, and route re-plans over the stated stops. Fulfilment and inventory. Stock below its reorder point, and the purchase orders that answer it. Cold chain. Temperature readings against stated limits. FACE never assumes a threshold the source did not provide. Maintenance and fleet. Predictive maintenance findings per vehicle. Invoices, deductions and contracts. Overbilling, duplicate invoices and deductions the documents do not support. Custody, customs and cover. Bills of lading, customs entries and insurance, checked before a file is bound or a claim is paid.
data.where-things-are-in-the-app#Where things:
The left rail is the only menu: three sections, with Settings at its foot.
Section Pages Fetch Ask, where the app opens, and Briefs. Cameras, devices, field readers and live sensors are connection types, opened from their card on Ask. Simulate Options and Why. Twins Actionable Twins: the decisions in lanes, with a Map view of the same decisions, site plans and twin entities as panels over the map, and Follow-ups. Foot Settings: Account, Personas, Integrations (channels, systems, contacts, runners) and Subscription. An assistant sits at the bottom right of every page, and a card narrates any run while it works. See Using FACE.

data:
This section describes the security controls FACE implements. It is written for the security reviewers, assessors and architects who have to decide whether FACE can hold their data.
Every page follows the same rule. It describes a control that exists in the code, names the setting, RPC or error text the control uses, and ends with the scope of the control: what it covers, and what stays with your deployment. If a property is not stated here, do not assume FACE has it. Ask us instead.
FACE is SOC 2-oriented in its design. These pages do not claim any certification, attestation or authorisation: SOC 2, ISO 27001, ISO 42001, FedRAMP, CMMC or ITAR. See Compliance posture for what that wording means and what it does not.
data.design-principles#Design principles: Fail closed at startup. FACE will not start without its mesh certificate authority, its at-rest key-encryption key, its session signing key, its encrypted application root and an inference endpoint. No fallback mode runs with any of these missing. No switch that turns a control off. Mesh mTLS, at-rest sealing and the instance-metadata refusal cannot be disabled by any environment variable. Sovereign inference. FACE calls no outside AI service on any plan. The text, vision and speech models run inside the deployment’s own cluster: Runink’s shared machines on Lite, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. The lineage log records structure, never values. It records which source was read, what shape came back and where it went. It never records the data itself. Say what a control does not do. A green check is worth only what it actually proves.
data.pages-in-this-section#Pages in this sect: Defence in depthAuthenticated, role-checked requests, mesh mTLS with rotating ECDSA identities, no plaintext downgrade. Identity & accessSessions, OIDC, MFA, allowlists, RBAC, and the exact unauthenticated surface. Encryption at restEnvelope encryption, the required KEK, sealed metadata, objects and credentials. Sovereign inferenceIn-cluster models, no third-party LLM API, and where data does leave. AI safetyPrompt fencing, OpenBias guardrails, the voice line, action judging, TOON output. Auditability & lineageAlways-on audit events, and an observed lineage log that carries no data values. Network egress controlsThe connector address policy, read-only SQL checks, and IPv6-first dialling. Compliance postureWhat SOC 2-oriented means here, and why the compliance env vars are declarations.
data.where-the-platform-ends-and-face-begins#:
FACE is an application running on the Runink platform. The platform provides the cluster, the edge that terminates browser TLS, certificate and secret delivery, the object store and the inference plane. These pages describe what the FACE backend enforces itself, together with the shared Runink libraries it links (security, store, mesh and inference). Where a property depends on how the platform is deployed, the page says so. Deployment and day-to-day operation are covered in Operations.
Scope of this section. It describes the code. It is not a penetration test or an audit report, and it says nothing about the deployment you run. Network policy, log retention, key custody and backups all belong to your installation, and you have to verify them there.

data: FACE’s agents read a customer’s records and propose actions. The controls on this page sit at the points where untrusted text reaches a model, and where a model’s output could turn into an action. None of them makes a language model safe against a determined adversary. Together they make attacks harder and bound what an attack can achieve, and each one says where it stops.
data.bounding-what-agents-may-do#Bounding wha:
A mitigation against injection has to be paired with limits on what model output can cause:
Agent email is always a draft. An email an agent composes is created as a draft in the operator’s mailbox for a person to read and send; no agent sends mail on its own, whatever FACE_AGENT_EMAIL_ALLOWLIST or the decision-authority policy says (see Auditability & lineage). Both are still evaluated, and the draft is audited with the recipient hashed, so the record shows what the policy would have allowed. Proposed actions are bounded. Every action an agent proposes is checked against that agent’s allowlist of action kinds and approver roles and its OpenBias rules before it is shown, high-risk action kinds (such as moving money) are refused for every agent, and links to hosts outside FACE_OUTPUT_URL_HOSTS are removed from answers. Nothing an agent proposes runs until a named person approves it.
